On the Orders of the Day being called:
I wish to repeat my inquiry of yesterday in regard to the disposition of the Hindu immigrants recently arrived at Vancouver. What steps have been taken towards their admittance or exclusion?

The Minister of the Interior is not here at the moment. I understand that all steps required by and in accordance with the law and the regulations made under the law have been taken and are being taken. I will ask the Minister of the Interior to give further information on the subject when there is an opportunity. I think I gathered from the minister's conversation that some twenty men who were not affected by the regulations, but who were returning to Canada, had been admitted; that certain physical tests appUed to some of the others would prevent their admittance, and that the law and the regulations made under the law would be enforced so far as the others are concerned.

The information I desired was whether the Government intended to rest their case on that provision of the immigration law which excludes appeal to the courts, or do they intend to permit an appeal to the courts? No doubt appeals to the courts will be made. Will the Government allow those appeals, or will they stand upon the letter of the statute?
The question is: Will the Government, if there is an appeal to the court, for instance, by way of habeas corpus, resist the application, or will they allow the habeas corpus to issue?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If any habeas corpus were applied for, the Government would be ready to proceed. If it would be a case in which a writ of habeas corpus should not be applied for, the Government would resist it to the best of their ability. Of course, my hon. friend understands that we cannot suggest and do not desire to control the action of the courts.

Certainly not; but, if I understood my hon. friend's question, it is: Does the statute as drawn prevent the issuing of a writ of habeas corpus so far as it can do so? No doubt the parties brought in who are British subjects will apply for a habeas corpus. The question is: Will the Government hold to the letter of the statute, or will they allow the habeas corpus to go through?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that in previous applications that point was taken and insisted upon; and of course we can insist upon it again.
On former occasions the Government did not resist the application, and as a result sixteen men were allowed in. As a further result these four hundred are now coming.

Consideration in 'Committee of resolutions respecting the Canadian Northern railway, resumed from Tuesday, May 26, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 14:
That no shares of the capital stock of the respective companies mentioned in the first schedule hereto, other than the Canadian Northern, beyond the amounts heretofore issued, shall be issued without the consent of the Governor in Council.

Why should that not
read 'without the consent of Parliament'? These constituent companies ace all to form part of the Canadian Northern Railway system and it has been stated over and over again by my hon. friend the Solicitor General that, whatever might be the shares of these constituent companies, they are to be represented by the stock of the Canadian Northern railway. Therefore there ought not to be any power vested in the Governor in Council to increase the capital stock of those companies. I do not see why they should be increased at all. It seems to me that there should be an absolute prohibition upon any increase, or, if there is to be an increase in the future, it should be by Act of Parliament. Discretion should not be vested in the Governor in Council in reference to the capital stock of these constituent companies. I would move that for the words * Governor in Council ' there should be substituted the words ' the Parliament of Canada

I cannot see what purpose can be effected by the amendment. The shares of the subsidiary companies pass into the treasury of the Canadian Northern railway and in that way a limitation is fixed on the total capitalization. Even if an increase were made I do not know that there is any likelihood of any difficulty arising because it does not increase the capital stock of the company.
I may draw attention also to this fact, that as the law now stands it is not the Parliament of Canada that consents to an increase in capitalization, but the Governor in Council. I do not see why an exception should be made here, especially as in this case the likelihood of an increase is much less than in the ordinary case. If it should be desirable to increase the capitalization of one of the subsidiary companies, the total capitalization of the united concern is not thereby increased at all. The precaution that is now taken, I think, is quite sufficient, and I submit -and I think my hon. friend will agree with me-that even if the clause passes as it stands, the approval of the Railway Commissioners would be a condition precedent to the consent of the Governor in Council. The ordinary law in the Railway Act would still apply.

Capitalization is created in two ways. One is by the issue of capital stock, and the other is by the creation of debentures or debenture stock. Parliament contemplates that the money
for any railway enterprise shall be raised in either one or other or both of these ways. I quite understand that if the bond issue were being reduced, these companies might be given the opportunity to increase their capital stock, but in this case it is proposed to increase the bond issue by Act of Parliament by the enormous sum of $45,000,000. This is the time when the capitalization should be decreased, and that is the object of the amendment of which I gave notice yesterday. We have before us in this paragraph the suggestion that the capitalization of these constituent companies may be increased by the Governor in Council. I do not think Parliament should vest that right in the Governor in Council. It is true that sometimes Parliament allows capital stock to be increased by the Governor in Council, but ordinarily Parliament reserves to itself the right to fix and limit the capital stock. These companies are being brought into the Canadian Northern system, and my hon. friend says that he cannot see any reason why there should be any increase. I ask, then, why under this clause explicit authority is given the Governor in Council to increase the capitalization? If the time should ever arise when it would be in the public interest to increase the capital stock of these constituent companies, they should come to Parliament where the matter could be fully discussed in the light of public opinion and a proper decision arrived at. I think it is very objectionable indeed to give power to the Governor in Council to increase the capital stock of the subsidiary or constituent companies.

I think the proposition on which the hon. gentleman bases his suggestion is not right. Ordinarily, Parliament does not reserve to itself the right to increase the capital stock. That is now v ithin the jurisdiction of the Railway Commissioners, who recommend to the Governor in Council, and the Governor in Council approves or disapproves. In this Bill we have gone further, and made an exception. We say it is important that the capital stock of the amalgamated-and I use the word not in its technical sense-company should be limited to $100,000,000, and that only by the consent of Parliament should that be increased. But the increasing of the capital of the subsidiary company is a mere domestic arrangement, resulting not at all in the increase of the profit-earning power of the amalgamated concerns, resulting not at all, I repeat, in the increase

of the capitalization of the amalgamated concern. Its capitalization alone has the right, if any capitalization has a right, to call for dividends. If any contingency should arise to make it necessary to increase the stock of a subsidiary company, it being a mere domestic arrangement, there is additional reason why the power should be given to the Governor in Council.
If it is a mere domestic arrangement why is power given to the Board of Railway Commissioners in the case of public utilities such as railways, telephones, etc.?

The hon. gentleman has missed my point. In this case all the subsidiary companies are united, and the total capitalization arrived at and made stationary and increasable only by the Parliament of Canada. Therefore, I say that the increasing of the capital of the subsidiary companies is a mere domestic arrangement for the united company. 1 do not say that in ordinary cases there is any domestic arrangement at all. In the ordinary case Parliament and the country is interested.
Is this proposal a domestic arrangement ?
This is a public arrangement; but the increasing of the capitalization of the companies embodied in the united company is a domestic arrangement of the united company.

My hon. friend has drawn a herring across the trail by introducing the term, ' domestic arrangement.' My hon. friend has stated that the capital stock of this enterprise has been limited to $100,000,000, but we find that the stock of the company has been increased from $77,000,000 to $100,000,000 and that the parent company is also the owner of $81,000,000 of stock in the constituent companies; so that this enterprise has now $100,000,000 of its own, and $81,000,000 of stock of the subsidiary companies. My hon. friend told us yesterday that this stock is not alive, that it has to remain in the treasury of the Canadian Northern, but to-day we find that this stock which my hon. friend says is to remain in the treasury of the Canadian Northern and which they have no power to sell-to which I disagree-can be increased for domestic or other purposes. Why should it be increased at all if it is to remain forever in the coffers of the Canadian Northern? According to my hon. friend, the stock is to remain 
in the treasury of the Canadian Northern as so many blocks of stone; but now we are giving the subsidiary companies power to apply to the Governor in Council for an increase in their capitalization. That would make their stock alive. This provision is not at all consistent with the argument advanced by my hon. friend yesterday that this stock was to be mobilized in the treasury of the Canadian Northern and never taken out. If the capitalization of these subsidiary companies is to be increased it is for some purpose, and the only purpose can be to draw dividends.

That may be, but my words are strictly correct still. If it does draw dividends it means that much less on something else. I give my right hon. friend credit for being perfectly sincere in his doubts on this matter. I will try and put it in another way to convince my hon. friend.
I am open to conviction.

My right hon. friend
still seems to think that the $68,000,000 of stock brought into the Canadian Northern and the $100,000,000 of stock in the Canadian Northern proper would all have the right to call for dividends. Suppose that we assume, which of course is not strictly correct, that all the stock has the right to earn five per cent interest. My hon. friend contends that the $68,000,000 that is brought into the treasury and the $100,000,000 is entitled to five per cent. The $68,000,000 at five per cent would produce a revenue of $3,600,000. That $3,600,000 goes into the treasury of the Canadian Northern so that it only leaves $1,400,000 more to earn to get five per cent on the other stock, or a total of $5,000,000 in dividends, which is five per cent on the $100,000,000 alone. When the $100,000,000 earns five per cent the other is earning nothing. But if the other is earning five per cent then there is only $32,000,000 of the $100,000,000 of earning stock left to get five per cent on. If we assume that the stock is entitled to five per cent, there can only be five per cent on the $100,000,000 earned no matter how you look at it. Well, then, the $100,000,000 is all that is entitled to earn a dividend. I am glad to see that my right hon. friend thf leader of the Opposition appreciates the way in which I am putting it.
And I appreciate what you do not put also.

If my right hon. friend suggests that I will try and meet his wishes. If we consider that five per cent is an adequate dividend that would amount to $5,000,000 which is five per cent on $100,000,000 and when that is earned, for dividend purposes, the $68,000,000 is wiped out. I connot imagine what would be the domestic contingency that would call for an increase in the capitalization of one of these companies, but even if the capital should be increased to $78,000,000
Who framed this clause to provide for it?

-what would be the
difference? The $100,000,000 still remains the capitalization of these united concerns and they are only entitled to five per cent on it. The public are not interested; it is a domestic concern. There is much less call here for interposing the Parliament of Canada between an increase and no increase than there is under the Railway Act. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) asked me who framed the clause. This clause was framed by the Government of Canada for the protection of the people of Canada.

I said that I appreciated fully what my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) was just arguing, and I told him also that I appreciated as well what he did not put before Parliament and the country. My hon. friend says that the company would only be able to pay dividends on $100,000,000. If the company produce a revenue of $10,000,000, that would be a dividend of ten per cent upon a capitalization of $100,000,000. But if the company instead of paying the dividend upon a capitalization of $100,000,000, drew it from a capitalization of $181,000,000, that would be a dividend of a little more than five per cent. This is a very old trick well known to those who assisted my 'hon. friend to draft these resolutions. My hon. friend told us that this company wants to have the stock restricted to $100,000,000 and nothing more and at the same time to have in their possession this additional stock amounting to $81,000,000 and to have power to increase it to any figure they think proper. What can be the object of that? If my hon. friend is sincere in his expressed desire to have the stock of this company limited to $100,000,000, and nothing else, I fail to see why there should be this provision under which the company, who are the owners of the stock, may come to the Government and ask to have the stock of the subsidiary companies amounting to $81,000,000 increased for some domestic reason. The reason is very obvious. It is a well known practice in finance, when dividends become so large as to disturb the public mind and provoke discussion, to increase the stock and reduce the rate of dividend and if that is not the object in this case I fail to see what the object ie.	.
The Solicitor General has repeated, perhaps forty times, that the stock of the subsidiary companies is wiped out by becoming the property of the Canadian Northern.
I never said that yet.
I wish to get at a basis of agreement with the Solicitor General.

I said that for purposes of dividends the whole stock was reduced to $68,000,000 and that this $68,000,000, for purposes of dividends, is being wiped out and $23,000,000 of stock is being substituted for it.

My hon. friend, at the
last moment, used the very words * wiped out for purposes of dividends.'
For purposes of dividends.	,

It is only for purposes of dividends then, I presume. The Canadian Northern is a corporate entity. Its ownership represents certain physical assets. Each of these subsidiary companies is a corporate entity and it has in its ownership certain physical assets. The physical assets of the Canadian Northern Railway Company are separate and distinct from the physical assets' of the subsidiary companies. The Canadian Northern has a certain amount of stock upon which the physical assets of that company may be presumed at some time to earn dividends and the more you increase the amount of that stock the more stock there is to look for dividends from the earnings upon the physical assets of the Canadian' Northern Railway Company. The same condition prevails absolutely in regard to the individual subsidiary companies. Each is a corporate entity, each has certain physical assets, each has certain rights of earning, and the stock of each has a right to claim dividends- on these earnings. The fact that the stock of these subsidiary companies is placed in the treasury of the Canadian Northern Rail-

way Company to form part of the security for the guarantee of $45,000,000 by this Government does not in. any degree change the relationship of the Canadian Northern Railway Company in its aright to earn dividends upon its physical assets or the right of these subsidiary companies to earn dividends upon their physical assets to the measure of the stock issued in respect of the Canadian Northern. Railway Company on the one hand and the subsidiary companies on the other. My point is that the contention which my hon. friend has put up that there is some change in relationship between these several companies because of this legislation is utterly fallacious and absolutely without foundation as far as the terms of these resolutions are concerned. If his intention is, as he has expressed it to the House1, then he should revise these resolutions in order to embody the same expression in the resolutions. He has not done this; he refuses to do it. The insertion of this section is plain evidence of the continuance as separate entities of these subsidiary companies with the right to earn dividends out of their operation for the benefit of their stock. There is no other purpose in1 providing for an increase in the stock of each of these companies except it be a means to draw more dividends and there is no reason in suggesting that the dividends of these subsidiary companies are in any way merged in the dividends of the Canadian Northern which is a separate corporate entity holding separate stock and entitled to separate earnings upon the physical assets of the company.
In further support of that contention, these resolutions provide that there may and shall, under certain conditions, be mortgages placed upon the subsidiary companies in consideration of moneys advanced through this guarantee. The interest on these advances must be provided out of the separate earnings of those subsidiary companies, or otherwise there is no sense in taking a mortgage upon them. At any rate there is no possibility of the interest on such a mortgage being provided for unless the subsidiary company upon which that mortgage is taken has a separate corporate entity, having separate physical assets and separate earning powers, with a view to profits upon the shares of that company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is a difference of
opinion between my hon. friend and myself on that point, and I do not know that we shall advance the argument very much by each one reiterating at great length his conclusions upon the subject. It has been taken for granted in this debate that consideration of the oustanding amount of stock will have a very great influence upon the fixing of railway rates in this country. I am not inclined to accept that view. Judging from principles which have been laid down	in this	country	and in	theUnited States, the	question	of rates islikely to Ibe determined in future by the amount of fixed charges which of course must be taken into consideration, and apart from that, by consideration of the physical value of the road and of the service it renders to the	public.	To my mind, it	is avery simple	matter;	the only	stock of	any
one of these companies which can get into the hands of the public is the stock of the Canadian Northern railway, and the argument, as I understand it is, that those who have purchased that stock at a certain price will be entitled to come to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada and claim that the rates should be fixed at such amount as will provide, not only for the fixed charges on the road but for a reasonable return upon the investment they have made in the stock. Let us see how that will work out. The stock of not one of these subsidiary companies ever can get into the hands of the public, under the provisions of the resolutioin as we understand them.

We will suppose, for the sake of argument, that the stock which already exists is provided by issuing capital into the hands of the public. Is. it the purpose of this section that further stock shall be issued or may be issued that would get into the hands of the public?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Certainly not, and it
cannot under the terms of this resolution as I understand them. We understand the resolution to mean that and nothing more nor less than that, and if it is not plain to my hon. friend it can be made plain. This stock of the subsidiary companies cannot get into* the hands of the public. A certain portion of the stock of the Canadian Northern may get into the hands of the public, and let us suppose that the holders should come with the representation that the rates should be so fixed as not only to provide for

interest charges but also to provide for reasonable return to them upon their stock. Let us say that dividends have been declared upon the stock of the subsidiary companies and that the earnings, would justify such dividends. What is the result? The result is that these dividends go into the treasury of the Canadian Northern railway and are available with the other earnings of that railway for the purpose of declaring a dividend, and when that dividend is declared it must, according to the premise, be a reasonable return, and therefore the earnings of that road plus the dividend to be derived from the stock of the subsidiary companies, according to the premise from which we start, never could amount to more than, a reasonable return upon the stogk at which Canadian Northern railway is capitalized. That is as clear to me as any proposition that has ever been debated in this House. This stock of the Canadian Northern railway does not reach the public. When they are considering the earnings of the whole system with respect to the provision of a reasonable return upon the stock in the hands of the public, they must take into consideration not only the direct earnings of the parent company but the: income derived from these dividends, which are really a part of those earnings, and therefore, in the net result, it is upon one hundred millions and one hundred millions alone that you must measure your case when you go to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada to determine the rates which will, according to the contention of hon. gentlemen opposite, justify the holders of the stock in asking that the rates shall be so fixed as to yield them a reasonable return.

Assuming that my right hon. friend is correct, this resolution simply provides for the transfer to His Majesty of the shares which are mentioned in the first part of the second schedule. Take for instance the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company:	there is authority by
statute to issue fifty million dollars of stock. Suppose that stock were issued to the extent of fifty millions, the only portion which by the terms of this resolution His Majesty would have a lien on would be ten million dollars, the forty millions would be entirely free from any charge under this resolution, because section 2, paragraph b, says:
Grant a first, fixed, and specific mortgage oi charge upon the shares mentioned in the first part of the second schedule hereto.
If you look at the first part of the second schedule, you will find that the amount of shares specifically mentioned, which is to go to His Majesty, is $10,000,000. Why should the Government ask this Parliament to authorize the Governor in Council to increase these shares when the very moment they are increased the extra shares.do not belong to His Majesty at all but to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and may be issued to the public and may therefore become shares on which dividends should and might be paid.
Does the hon. gentleman think that the Canadian Northern Ontario Company is in any different position from those named in the first part of- the second schedule ?

I do not think there is any difference, but I took that for an example. Take the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan: although there are bonds to the extent of five million dollars against that road the share capital is only $201,000. There has been no inconvenience in the stock being for such a small amount except as an argument to go before the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, or as an argument to go to the investors. If you are dealing with the matter simply from the standpoint of a domestic arrangement, it makes no difference whether the capital stock of the company is one hundred thousand or one hundred million or ten thousand dollars, but it is when you go to the Board of Railway Commissioners and you are asking the board to allow you to impose a burden upon the people of Canada in the way of tolls, that it becomes important as to the amount of the capital stock. So, when you go to the investor and ask him to invest in shares, it is important what is the amount of the capital stock. The Solicitor General says it is merely a matter of domestic arrangement, and it cannot make the slightest difference to the public what is the amount of the capital stock, as amongst the shareholders themselves it is purely a question of proportion and division. This idea that it is beyond possibility that some reason might be advanced in the future why the capital stock of the constituent companies should be increased strikes me .as absurd; and the hon. gentleman will never make me believe that txiis clause was framed by the Government of Canada. It was framed, I believe, by Mr. Lash, the very able solicitor and counsel of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Mr. Lash is a far-seeeing man; and.

looking ahead and realizing what burdens the people of the West can bear with the resources of that great country and what earnings it may be .possible to wrench from those people, he foresees that the time may come when it will be desirable to increase these issues on the plea of re-funding the securities of the road and to go to the public with a vast amount of new capital stock which investors may be asked to subscribe for. For instance, the capital of the Canadian Northern Ontario may be in creased from $10,000,000 to $50,000,000, and that of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan which now has issued $201,000, representing 250 miles of road, might be increased to $3,000,000 or $4,000,000; and so with all these companies. He might well then come to the Government and to Parliament and say: We have got through the Governor in Council an increase in the capital stock of these constituent companies to $200,000,000 or $300,000,000, and now we want to make a re-issue; we want to re-fund the securities and consolidate all these loans into one system, wiping out the stoek of all these constituent companies; and he might well ask this Parliament to increase the capital stock of the company from $100,000,000 to $200,000,000 or $300,000,000, which might be represented by the existing stock of the Canadian Northern railway and by the increased stock of these constituent companies. And if he could get into the Government a gentleman, so ingenious and able as my hon. friend the Solicitor General, he might be able to persuade the majority of Parliament that that would be just the correct thing to do, just as he has succeeded in doing in this case. He has succeeded in persuading a trustful majority of Parliament, not over-zealous for the public interest-I will not say much of that, but it is a trustful majority-that this legislation is right. But, when we are increasing the fixed charges upon this road, when we are increasing the possibilities of laying burdens upon the people who have to use the road to get their products to market, when we are adding water to the extent of $50,000,000 to the stock of the Canadian Northern railway, why should we give to the Governor in Council the power to yield to the request of these gentlemen who control the Canadian -Northern railway and increase the capital stock of these constituent companies?

Would the hon. gentleman be pleased to say where that three-fifths comes in? Will he excuse my extreme

ignorance and tell me how he argues at one' moment that Mackenzie and Mann have taken a three-fifths share, and at the next that they have added $68,000,000?

I would not say that
the hon. gentleman's ignorance is extreme. Eelatively it is no greater than has been displayed in other quarters in this House. Therefore he does not do himself justice when he suggests that his ignorance is extreme. This matter, it strikes me, is of very serious importance to the people. The Solicitor General talks of it as a 'domestic arrangement.' But, when you are dealing with a great transportation system, you are not dealing with a mere matter of domestic arrangement between the shareholders themselves. The difficulty that arises is this. If you have the capital stock of these constituent companies increased, then, when they come to the Board of Eailway Commissioners and ,say:	We have a certain
amount of stock of the parent company, but we have a large amount of stock of these various constituent companies which have been paid for, which has ibeen earned by Mackenzie and Mann by the sweat of their brows and the wearing out of their intellects, which represents years of toil and the expenditure of a vast amount of money which it is not possible for one representing the Government to arrive at, the result of that appeal may be a very serious matter for the public. Therefore, I
12 noon, appeal to the hon. the Solicitor General. I know how difficult it is for him to yield to a suggestion of the Opposition. There are reasons which make him feel that he would sooner be wrong and continue wrong than to admit that a member on this side could put forward a suggestion that is worthy of consideration. But let me appeal to him to rise to the consideration of what is in the public interest and to declare now that the stock of these constituent companies shall not be increased at any time unless and until they come to Parliament, where the reasons can be given and the matter can be discussed in the eyes of the people, and a conclusion arrived at which will be in the public interest. That is all that I am asking for, so far as my amendment is concerned- that they shall not be able to go in secret to the Governor in Council and get this increase, but that if they want the increase they shall come to Parliament and have the reasons presented and the matter fully

discussed by the representatives of the people.

Before the
Solicitor General speaks, I would ask him whether, in view of the fact that there is now before Parliament a Bill to regulate the capitalization of railway companies, the provision placing the regulation of capitalization in the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioners will apply to this legislation now before the House or not, or whether this legislation will be outside of the general provision that is to be in the Railway Act.

Answering first the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean): The provisions as to capitalization as they are now framed in the proposed Railway Act would doubtless apply here; that is to say, any provision placing restriction upon an increase of capitalization in the new revised Act would apply here and place restrictions here. But, at the same time, the provision made here that no increase of the capitalization of the company from $100,000,000 shall be made without the consent of Parliament would not in any way be affected by the proposed revised Act.
Answering next the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley): I have not paid much attention heretofore to taunts as to Mr. Lash having framed this Bill, as to being seduced, as to being domineered, as to being mesmerized, as to being befooled, I leave the merits of the Bill to answer all that. The hon. member for the city of St. John proceeds on the assumption that increase of capitalization of a public utility such as a railway is a tremendous burden on the people of Canada.
Increase by water.

He thinks that increase of capitalization is a tremendous burden, and' he does not feel that that increase should be allowed in the future except by consent of Parliament. There is no anticipation that the stock will be increased by water any more than the stock of any other road will be increased by water. The laws of the country apply to these just the same as they apply to any others as to the methods by which they may increase their capital stock. But here is a clause which provides that the capitalization of the subsidiary companies shall not be increased except by consent of the Governor in Council, and there is another opposite it which says that capitalization of the united company shall not be increased except by
the consent of Parliament. But, my hon. friend says, because you say that the capitalization of the subsidiary companies shall not be increased except by consent of the Governor in Council, you framed the Bill under the dictation of Z. A. Lash. I want to ask the hon. gentleman who framed the Railway Act of Canada when he was Minister of Public Works? Who framed the Naval Service Act when he was Minister of Public Works?
When was the Railway Act framed?
The Railway Act was passed by the late Government, of winch the hon. gentleman was a member.
The Act was framed, not when I was minister, but some time before that. It was consolidated, I believe, by a commission in 1907.
It was framed before the hon. gentleman was minister, but it was consolidated and ratified while he was Minister of Public Works.
Consolidated by a commission.

Consolidated and ratified and had the supreme sanction of the hon. gentleman's intelligence in 1907. Here is the way the Railway Act provides for increase of capital stock, section 85:
The original capital stock of the companies may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, he increased from time to time to any amount if such increase is sanctioned by a vote, in person or by proxy, of the shareholders who hold at least two-thirds in amount of the subscribed stock of the comapny, at a meeting expressly called by the directors for that purpose, and the proceedings of such meetings have been entered in the minutes of the proceedings of the company.
The Railway Act provides that the capital stock may be increased by the consent oi the Governor in Council. As to the subsidiary companies, we have not altered the Railway Act in that respect. If this section of the resolution was framed by Z. A. Lash, who wrote this clause in the Railway Act? We have interposed the Parliament of Canada between any increase of the only capital stock in which we are concerned, the stock of the united company and the present capital stock, and to that extent we have moved forward; to that extent we have imposed restrictions. We have no object in placing restrictions on the others beyond those placed upon them by the Railway Act. I know that I cannot clarify the matter any

more by further repetition and I hope the hon. gentleman will do himself the justice of saying that there is at least no more evidence of Z. A. Lash in the proposed Bill than there is in the Bill which he ratified in 1907.

There is a
great deal.

Why not accept the
amendment of the hon. member for the city of St. John? It has been said that it is probable that the stock of the subsidiary companies will be increased.
I do not think so.

I do not.think so myself, but I cannot possibly see why the Solicitor General objects to the amendment of my hon. friend. It cannot possibly make any difference; it is not likely that they will want to increase the amount of their stock, as it is controlled by the parent company, but why not make them come to Parliament if they do want to increase it? The hon. gentleman referred to the Railway Act, but I would point out that this is special legislation, altogether outside of the Railway Act
The hon. gentleman will admit at once that if it makes no difference at all, there is no reason for accepting the amendment.

I did not mean it that
way; my hon. friend takes me up wrongly. I say that it makes no difference to the subsidiary companies if you make them come back to the Parliament of Canada if they intend to increase their stock.

If it is an improvement to compel the railway companies before they increase their capital stock to come to the Parliament of Canada, the way to effect that improvement is by general legislation. If there "were any special reason for such action in this case, I would admit that it should be done, but there is no special reason in the case of the capital of the united company, and there is no special reason in the case of the others. There is rather less reason, because the profits on that stock necessarily go into the treasury of the united company and the country is interested only in the stock of the united company.

There is n,o reason why
all railway companies should not come to Parliament if they wish to increase their capital stock
Then it should be done under the General Railway Act,

I will give a reason why there should be a regulation in this regard, and to do so I will refer to the experience of the previous Government. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, taking advantage of existing legislation, applied to the Governor in Council for an increase of ite capital stock, and they got that increase very much against the public opinion of this country and very much against the interests of those who use the railway and pay railway rates. We all know that when the protest was made in the press and on the platform that the Canadian Pacific Tailway had unfairly increased its capital stock, we were told that it had been done by consent of the Governor in Council. On a subsequent occasion, during the administration of the present Government, the Canadian Pacific railway increased its stock without the consent of the Governor in Council, and nothing was done. I consider that increase to have been a public scandal, and against the establishment of reasonable railway rates in this country. 1 am altogether in favour of having absolute control of the capitalization of all companies operating railways, and I think that this company, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and every other railway company, should be subject to regulations by Parliament acting on its own motion, or by Parliament acting through the Railway Commission. If I read aright a declaration made on behalf of the Canadian Pacific railway yesterday in the Montreal press, it is that there is to be an immense segregation of the extraneous assets of that company and subsidiary companies. That means that the earnings of these subsidiary companies will, in a way, be separated from the earnings of the general company. I am loth to think that this session is to close without Parliament taking control of the capitalization of all our railways. If we are not to pass a Bill amending the general Railway Act, I hope that a provision regulating the capitalization of railways will be made law this session, and that it will be applicable, as the Solicitor General says, to all subsidiary companies, though not to the consolidated company, which is subject to a special provision regarding capitalization. I think that when we regulate the capital stock of the Canadian Northern, and put it under the control of Parliament or of a commission

named by Parliament, we should at the same time include not only the Canadian Northern, but all other railways as well; because we are admitting now the principle -and it is high time we did-that control of the capitalization of railways should be in the hands of 'Parliament or of its nominees. If we do not do this we will see something between now and the next session. The Canadian Pacific railway has slipped by this Parliament on two or three occasions, increases in its capital, sometimes by way of an Ordeir in Council, sometimes by legislation which it says it got passed years ago. In this way it was able only a year ago to increase its capital stock against the public interest. So it is the duty of Parliament this session, to regulate the capitalization of the Canadian Northern railway and the subsidiary companies and also to regulate the capitalization of all companies, and so there .should come, with equal step with this Bill now before us, .a public Bill putting the control of the capitalization! ot all our railway companies in the hands of Parliament. I do not agree with what the Prime Minister said a moment ago that capitalization has very little to do with railway rates. I believe that it has had a lot to do with it, and all the. arguments that are put up in favour of the increase of railway rates, the argument being put up now in the States in favour of an increase in railway rates,is' largely based on the idea of capitalization invested, although a lot of the money was unfairly taken away from the undertakings and fell into the hands of speculators of various kinds. Therefore I say it is in the public interest that the capitalization of all railways, the Canadian Northern railway, the Canadian Pacific railway and all other roads, should be placed in the hands of Parliament. And it should be placed in the hands of Parliament this session. . We should not postpone the general Act to another .session and thereby leave all the other roads free to do as they please.

I am very glad to hear from my hon. friend who has just taken his seat that he is in favour of Parliament controlling the capitalization of the company. I am especially glad, or shall be especially glad, if by his vote he gives expression., in the most emphatic and practical way that it can be given, to those views, because we are now asked to legislate especially in respect to some fifteen or sixteen subsidiary companies, and all I am asking by my amendment is that the capital of these companies shouild not be increased except with the consent of Parliament. That is the very thing I am asking for, and if there was ever a case where Parliament should be allowed to exercise that authority it is in the present case, because these companies to-day have an issued capital stock of about $68,000,000. The Government is providing, as they assure us, that these shares shall go into the treasury of the Canadian Northern railway, that they shall lose all life and vitality and shall be held there in the treasury, that they shall not represent anything so far as paying dividends is concerned, that they shall represent nothing at all except that they are to be used for the purpose of keeping alive these various constituent companies. That can be accomplished as well with $1,000,000 as it can with $68,000,000. Yet, notwithstanding these assurances, the Government comes to us to-day with a clause with which the Solicitor General says that Mr. Lash, that wicked man, had nothing in the world to do-he does not use the words ' wicked man ' but suggests that I called him one because he had pulled the wool over the eyes of my hon. friend, which would be a very wicked and indefensible thing to do. When, notwithstanding that these subsidiary companies have this $68,000,000 of issued stock to-day, which he says is to be used in the way I speak of, and when he asks power in this Parliament to the Governor in Council, upon a secret . application, of which the public would not have knowledge, to increase the capital stock of these constituent companies, all that we are saying on. this side of the House is that that power shall be vested in the Parliament of Canada. That is all. Parliament represents the people of the country. All we .ask is that if at any time it should be deemed desirable for any reason to increase the issued shares of these companies, they should be compelled to come to Parliament, to present their reasons so that the public might know what those reasons are and so that the members of this Parliament might be enabled to judge whether or not the reasons are sound. In the case to which my hon. friend refers, of an ordinary railway company, the capital stock it is true can be increased; but when Parliament passed that law, by the Railway Act, it contemplated, what Parliament always contemplates, that there would be a bona fide sub-

script-ion for stock in those companies. But to-day we have it admitted practically that all this $68,000,000 of stock is watered stock, represents nothing except, as I have said, the mental toil of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann; that is all it represents. It does not represent, so far as we know, a dollar of money. Therefore, if there ever was a reason why Parliament should have the control of the increase of capital stock of railway companies, it exists in respect of these companies to-day. Therefore, it does seem to me that it is entirely reasonable and entirely in the public interest, if it is desired to increase the capital stock of these companies, that they should be obliged to come to Parliament in order to get authority to make the proposed increase. Amendment of Mr. Pugsley negaJtived: yeas, 29; nays, 44.

Section agreed to.
On section 16:
That while any of the guaranteed securities are outstanding the Governor in Council may from time to time appoint any person to be a director of any or of all the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern system, and at pleasure remove the director so appointed.
2. Every director appointed by the Governor in Council shall at the request of the Governor in Council have the right to have a meeting of the directors or shareholders of the company for which he is so appointed,. called at any time, and the secretary or- other proper officer of such company shall at such company's expense forthwith upon being requested so to do, call such meeting in accordance with the statutes or by-laws regulating the calling thereof.

Why should this right
be limited to the period during which the guaranteed securities are outstanding? If the Government is to remain a shareholder! to the extent of two-fifths why should it not still continue to have the right to appoint a director at pleasure?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Government can still exercise its influence, the same as any other shareholder, after the period mentioned.

Section agreed to.
On section 17:
That without limiting any power now possessed, it be enacted that any railway company comprised in the Canadian Northern system which is now or may hereafter be subject to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada may, with the approval of the Governor m Council, enter into arrangements and agreements with any other railway company comprised in the said system which is now or may hereafter be subject to said legislative authority, or which has now, or may hereafter have power

to enter into the same, respecting the operation by or the leasing to or the sale and transfer to such other railway company of the undertaking of the first mentioned company including assets, rights, franchises and powers, and said companies are hereby respectively empowered to carry out such arrangements and agreements.

I want to point out that
this and subsequent clauses contemplate the preservation of the entities of the subsidiary companies.
Is that the intention of the Government, or does it contemplate the absorption of all these companies into one system with central control?	,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think I mentioned in
presenting the resolution to the House in< the first instance that in the opinion of the Government it was desirable to have all these lines pass into the ownership of one, system, but that by reason of the various financial arrangements which had been made it did not seem practicable to do that at the present time. Therefore, we have done the next best thing by providing that the stock of all these companies shall pass into the Canadian Northern. While that arrangement continues, it would seem that the provisions made in this and the preceding section will serve to carry out the purpose of the resolutions in that respect, namely, the amalgamation so far as practicable of all these lines into one system.

I would favour the amalgamation of the system, but it strikes me that there is room for a measure of financial juggling in the provisions of these three sections. I think that the amalgamation that is proposed to take place should be subject to the responsibility of the Government, so that we might protect whatever private or public interests might be involved. We are giving legislative authority to these subsidiary companies-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, and the proposal in the next section is subject to the approval of the Governor in Council and to the provisions of the Railway Act.

Section agreed to.
On section 19:
That any company now or hereafter comprised in the Canadian Northern system which is now or may hereafter be subject to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, may acquire shares in the capital stock of, or securities issued by, or make advances to, or receive advances from any other company comprised in said system, and may take or give security for such advances.

What does that mean? By another clause, all the shares in these constituent companies are vested in the Canadian Northern. That being so, how can any one constituent company acquire shares in another constituent company as this clause provides?

I do not see how it could acquire shares except in the case of a new issue authorized by the Governor in Council. In the event of one subsidiary company making a new issue this clause enables the Governor in Council to direct that the issue may go to another company.
It does not say that.

There could be no other case in which they could acquire shares because the stock is all owned by the Canadian Northern and is to remain in its treasury. Therefore, this must apply to a new issue. I do not know what domestic contingency might call for that.
If the hon. gentleman drafted this section he ought to know what it is for.

I know what it means, but I do not know the domestic contingency that might call for its exercise. I see that the parent company could acquire the shares of a new issue by a subsidiary company authorized by Order in Council, and I would say that if such a new issue were authorized it would be the desire of the parent company to acquire it.
It does not say the parent company.
It would appear to me to be most likely that the parent company would acquire the issue.
Is it contemplated that the stock of these subsidiary companies shall be owned by any other company than the Canadian Northern?

No. This is to provide that the parent or another company may acquire new stock, and I can only conceive of the parent company doing that. It has been the practice of the parent company hitherto to make advances to the subsidiary companies and that may, and perhaps will, be necessary in the future.

Assuming that the Canadian Northern desired to purchase another road; the Quebec and Saguenay, for instance. I understand that by this Bill they would have the power to purchase any other
road. Is there anything to prevent the stock of the Quebec and Saguenay road being transferred to one of the constituent or subsidiary companies and not to the parent company itself ? It seems to me this clause is strong enough to allow of that manipulation taking place. I know my hon. friend will say that it all boils down to the $100,000,000, and if that is correct it would not make much difference. But is not the clause sufficiently broad to allow of such a transfer to the subsidiary or constituent companies ?

It would appear to me that if the taking over of the Quebec and Saguenay had been first authorized by the Governor in Council, as provided for in the introductory part of the Bill, the shares of stock in that road might be acquired by a subsidiary company; but, as I say, the ultimate result would be the same.

For what purpose does my hon. friend provide for the issue of stock by any of these companies ? He argued yesterday, and again this morning, that the stock of these constituent companies was wiped out for all practical purposes. Why, then, permit the creation of new stock which, if there is anything in the hon. gentleman's argument, would also be wiped out ? My hon. friend must have had something in mind in drafting that provision. I can conceive of rights being reserved giving power to make advances. That is one thing, but in view of that, all that has been urged in regard to this question of stock from the beginning, on what possible ground can my hon. friend provide that there may be an issue of stock by these companies ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The section deals not only with the acquisition of shares hut with the acquisition of securities as well. Altogether apart from the aid that is now being afforded, it might be possible at some time in the future, and before the companies are all amalgamated into one, that the Canadian Northern railway would have to make advances to one of the subsidiary companies for the purpose of enabling the line to be put in better condition or for the purpose of enabling it to extend its system-. In that case this section provides that either by the transfer of shares, or by the transfer of securities to be issued by the subsidiary companies, the Canadian Northern Railway Company can deal with the situation and can make the advances necessary for the purpose. That is one object that strikes me at the moment. It is

impossible to foresee all contingencies. I dare say there may be other contingencies which might suggest themselves if one were thoroughly conversant with the operations of railway companies.

That is just the very
point that we have been arguing all morning and a part of last evening. What the right hon. gentleman has said is the very opposite of the argument presented by the Solicitor General who is contending that it makes no difference what the capitalization of the subsidiary or allied companies may be because all their stock, whether it be $68,000,000, or $81,000,000, or whether it be another $400,000,000, becomes merged into, and becomes the property of, the Canadian Northern Railway Company, the capital stock of which is reduced down to $100,000,000. My right hon. friend now says that the Canadian Northern railway may have to advance money to one of the subsidiary companies and that therefore they ought to have a right to take stock as security. What reason can there be for that if the Canadian Northern owns the whole thing and if the Canadian Northern stock is limited to $100,000,000 as the Solicitor General says it is? The Solicitor General says that under no contingency is it possible that the stock on which they can demand dividends can exceed $100,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Canadian Northern,
for the purpose of making these advances, would probably, itself, have to issue securities which would be placed on the market. They could be issued by the Canadian Northern very much more advantageously than they could be placed on the market by one of tnese companies. Therefore, it may be a good financial arrangement for the Canadian Northern to issue its own securities for the purpose of making provision for one of the subsidiary companies and it may take the stock or securities of the subsidiary company to compensate' it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It may not take stock; it m&y take securities. In any case the Canadian Northern is capitalized at a fixed amount and if it was to take shares it would take these shares subject to the consideration already referred to.

Such shares would
have no commercial value.

speechtext:
Except as giving the
Canadian Northern a very much increased

interest. They would not necessarily take shares; they might take securities.

If the Solicitor General be correct in his argument that under this Bill every equity which these companies possess, including all their stock certificates and everything, goes to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, how can the Canadian Northern Railway Company take any further security by way of stock, or bonds, or anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I must confess I do not see why they cannot.

What is the good of it, because the Canadian Northern owns it now? It just makes one believe that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has opened up something which has not been explained away. What had the gentleman who drafted this clause in his mind? If it was the Solicitor General he ought to be able to tell us. If it was not the Solicitor General I think he should get into communication with the gentleman who drafted this clause and ascertain what his real intention was. The more the right hon. the Prime Minister attempts to explain 'it the more difficult he makes it for the Solicitor General.

I have explained what the meaning of the clause is. I have said I cannot tell what the intention of the company is; I do not pretend to he able to tell that. I do not pretend to be a railway expert and to know all the contingencies that may arise, but I do know that under that clause they cannot do anything prejudicial to the public interest. If hon. gentlemen can suggest anything that may be done prejudicial to the public interest, and suggest a remedy for it, we will be glad to consider it.

If there is any object in issuing additional shares of this stock it may be prejudicial to the public interest because if the line ever becomes a paying investment there may be a demand that these shares shall receive dividends. If my hon. friend is serious in saying that these shares never can demand dividends, but that the only dividend demanding shares will be the $100,000,000 of stock owned by the parent company, then I would suggest the amending of this section by striking out the word * shares.' The right to issue other securities, like bonds or debenture stock, might not be very serious but if he would eliminate the word ' shares ' he would get rid of the suspicion

we have notwithstanding the oft-repeated assertion of the learned Solicitor General that there may he some real object in the mind of the Canadian Northern people in keeping the shares of these subsidiary companies in their own hands.

If by merely eliminating the -word ' shares ' we could get rid of the suspicion in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite, I would be inclined to do it; but I do not think it is so important as that, and I am not very hopeful that we could eradicate from the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite at least the allegation of suspicion.
Make toe attempt and see how you will succeed.

I cannot see what harm can result if it is convenient for the Canadian Northern on one part of the system to take shares on another part; nor can I see what harm can be done if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that it would be in the interests of the Canadian Northern system to, say, amalgamate one portion of the road with another and give stock. Everything is under the control of the Governor in Council just the same as everything is under the control of the Railway Act. The capital is $100,000,000 and it cannot be increased. If a new road should be acquired the arrangement is under the control of the Governor in Council and the Railway Commission. There is no change from the Railway Act in this respect at all. Has the hon. gentleman lost faith-in the Railway Commission?

There might be a
possible explanation in connection with this section. If one will examine the first schedule he will find that the statement is made with respect to the Canadian Northern Manitoba Company, The Mount Royal Terminal Company and some others, that the security is to be the total issue. Has any issue of stock been made by these companies?

No, not by either of
them.

How much is it to be
made?

I do not know and I
cannot see what imaginable difference it makes. It is to belong to the Canadian Northern system out and out whatever it is. If it is $50,000,01)0 it belongs; if it is $200 it belongs.
