Assuming that the Canadian Northern system purchases the Quebec and Saguenay that road will have a capitalization of $5,000,000 and they will buy the stock. I take it for granted that that would increase the stock of the Canadian Northern by $5,000,000 so that the stock of the Canadian Northern would be be $105,000,000 if the stock were purchased by the Canadian Northern itself. If purchased by one of the original companies it would go in as part of the original transaction, but if the Canadian Northern purchased, am I right in assuming that the stock would be increased by five million dollars, and if so would the Government get two-fifths, or would it all go to the Canadian Northern?

I think the hon. gentleman is a little confused; I do not think he quite appreciates what would take place. I would say that, in so far as the acquisition of the new road is concerned, we are just in the same position as we are generally under the Railway Act. lit could not be acquired and stock given for it except with the consent of the Governor in Council. Stock cannot be given for it because it cannot be issued to be given except with the consent of the Governor in Council, and the Governor in Council would say whether it should be five million dollars or two hundred thousand dollars. If it were deemed in the interest of the system, which would be in our interest and in the interest of the public, and the Governor in Council agreed to approve of the issue of whatever sum might be deemed proper for the acquisition of another Tailway, and the stock went there, where would be the injury done? In so far as the assets we bring into this system now are concerned, it will never go beyond one hundred million dollars. But there is some stock outstanding even yet that does not come into the system, and that stock is in the same position as before. Similarly, if any issue should be made, and so far as I know none is contemplated, it must be approved by the Governor in Council; it must be deemed adequate for the advantage attained! by the issue of it, and consequently the public interest is protected in the same way as it is protected under the Railway Act.
My hon. friend has not answered my question, but as I understand it he admits that the capital stock of the parent company would have to be increased.
If it is the parent company it would have to be with the consent of the Parliament of Canada, and, if a subsidiary company, with the consent of the Governor in Council.

* 1 asked the Solicitor General if the stock were increased, would the people of Canada get any proportion of it or would it all go to the Mackenzie and Mann interests. Suppose the Quebec and Saguenay were purchased, the people of Canada would have to stand behind it and foot the bill, as I understand n.

Suppose there is another railway, which is worth one million dollars we will say, and it is deemed advisable in the interests of the system that that railway be acquired for one million dollars stock of the Canadian Northern Ontario railway, the company has to come to the Governor in Council just the same as it would come under the Railway Act, just as it lias come all along. And if it were deemed by the Government of Canada in the interest of the people that that road *be acquired, it would be acquired the same as it would be under the Railway Act and the stock would issue. That means an increase of assets and another road added to the system. There is no increase of the capitalization on what we are getting now; that is impossible.

All these subsidiary
companies remain under the direction of directors appointed by Mackenzie and Mann.
By the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

The directors would be nominees of Mackenzie and Mann. I assume from the reading of clause 3 that the Government does not intend to interfere in any way with the management of these constituent companies until, at all events, there is default. Section 19, which is of the broadest possible character, reads:
That any company now or hereafter comprised in the Canadian Northern system which is now or may hereafter be subject to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, may acquire shares in the capital stock of, or securities issued by, or make advances to, or receive advances from any other company comprised in said system, and may take or give security for such advances.
That system is composed of the Canadian Northern and some fourteen or fifteen constituent companies. Let me point out to the Solicitor General that under this section power is given to the directors [Mr. Carvell.j
of the Canadian Northern or any constituent company to acquire and become owners of outstanding stock of the Canadian Northern. They could acquire the stock Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, hold in the Canadian Northern. I cannot imagine that is intended, and yet the power is given under this section. If this proposition goes through, Mackenzie and Mann will own sixty million of this stock, and power is given to the directors of any one of these companies, without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners and without the consent of the Governor in Council, to buy the whole or a part of that stock in the Canadian Northern which is held by Mackenzie and Mann, Limited. Did my hon. friend have that in view when he drew this section?

I do not think I had
anything quite so imaginary as that in view.	.'
What was it then?
What would be the object of the directors of a subsidiary company, who are appointed by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, buying the shares of the Canadian Northern Railway Company?
It is owned by Mackenzie and Mann and would foe so much money in their pockets.

Very well, and if they
did how would we be affected? I can see no object in doing it, but if they did how would the country be affected? Mackenzie and Mann can dispose of their shares to anybody.
Why give a constituent company power to buy the shares?
The Canadian Northern owns it if the constituent company buys it. The constituent company is owned by the Canadian Northern.

If that is so, then if
the Canadian Northern Ontario, through a board of directors nominated by Mackenzie and Mann, thought it desirable to acquire ten million dollars stock in the parent company-Mackenzie and Mann hold the ten million dollars stock-and they buy it for five million dollars; the Canadian Northern Ontario is a subsidiary company going through a rich part of Ontaro and they may have some money.
The hon. member from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) says its stock is all watered.

I do not know that any one will deny that, but suppose they would like to get a little of this stock in the parent company and become partners also. This clause allows them to do so by paying out of the earnings of the Canadian Northern railway 810,000,000 or $5,000,000, as the case may be, for this stock. What is the result? It puts $5,000,000 or $10,000,000 into the pockets of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and gives to the constituent companies stock which may or may not be of very much advantage to the parent company. Is not this a dangerous power? I think it is. It is contended that it is a useful power. I think not. If the hon. gentleman framed this clause, he can tell us what was his intention in drawing it and what is the object sought.

I have already stated the intention and object and circumscription of the clause. As to the contingency the hon. gentleman has in mind, it is this, that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, might sell their stock to the Canadian Northern Ontario, which is owned by the Canadian Northern railway, sell it at fictitious value, and thus get money into their own pockets and out of the Canadian Northern Ontario. Well, fraud is always possible. Mackenzie, Mann and Company might sell a horse to the Canadian Northern railway for $10,000,000, and the horse might not be worth that much. You cannot frame clauses to prevent transactions of that kind; such a difficulty is inherent in the management of any company.
Would the clause give that power if they chose to exercise it?
I see no reason why it should not.

The Solicitor General's position in regard to the clause is: I do not know what this power is that we are conferring upon these companies to deal with shares; I cannot tell why it is put there; but I want to know from you gentlemen of the Opposition what harm it is and how it can prejudice the country-if you cannot show that, it ought to go in. But as he assumes the responsibility, we are told, for the drafting of these resolutions, his duty is to tell the committee what the meaning of the clause is and why he put it there.

I have done that, but perhaps it is no more than courteous that I should do it again. I stated it to the hon. member for Carleton, N. B. (Mr. Car veil). I suggested the possibility of acquiring a new line necessitating the issue of stock of the Canadian Northern Ontario for it, in which case the Governor in Council must pass an order that the new line is part of the system, fixing the amount of the new issue and the conditions under which it is to be made. As to making advances, I do not need to explain that to him-
That is not the point.
No, the point is in regard to shares. But I made the explanation in reply to the suggestion of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., making clear what the purpose is-
I am sorry it does not make it clear to me; probably that is my fault.

It is an imaginary
possibility, but according to the Solicitor General the clause gives power to go on and construct new railways in the cases he proposes-
I did not say ' construct ' new railways; I spoke of the purchase of a railway.

Why is the power
given for purchasing and what new railways is it contemplated to purchase?

I have stated that none are contemplated, so far as I know. But this clause gives the Governor in Council power to add anjther company to the system, if the Governor in Council thinks it wise. One way it can be added is by the issue of shares of the Canadian Northern Ontario. This clause would provide for that.
That is pure'y imaginary.
This provides for the issue of additional shares.

Yes, when authorized
by the Governor in Council.

What is the position of
these shares in relation to revenue.
The same as the others. There is new property for them.
But as to dividends, would they be drawing dividends or would they not?

It would take a prophet to say that.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

The hon, Solicitor General said, as I understood him, that there is no doubt that if section 19 passes it will be quite open to any one of these eighteen constituent companies to purchase stock of the Canadian Northern and it will be quite possible for them to make purchases of a portion' of the stock of Mackenzie. Mann and Company, Limited. But my hon. friend .suggests that that wouild be fraud, particularly if they bought the stock for more than its market value. Until the stock is earning a dividend .and is listed on the stock exchange, thereby getting a market value, opinions may differ very greatly as to its value and the directors of one of these subsidiary companies, who are to-day and will be the nominees of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, may take a different view of the value of that stock from that taken by others. I do not know that it would necessarily be fraud if one of these constituent companies should acquire a considerable block of that stock and utilize the funds of one or more of these subsidiary companies for that purpose. It would not be fraud to do the thing itself, because Parliament. has expressly provided that any one or more of these constituent companies may purchase the stock of any of the others. This clause may not be acted upon, but certainly if it passes it opens up possibilities of entanglements which may operate prejudicially to the public interest and which will require two or three gentlemen equally astute as the Solicitor General to unravel. The hon. Solicitor General has developed such ability in unravelling the entanglements which now exist in reference to this matter that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance said that he would take off his hat to him. If this clause is acted upon by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, under the wide flowers which are thereby conferred, it will take even .greater ability to untangle the difficulties if the matter comes again before the Government and before Parliament. Why put it in? Where is the necessity for it?

Why give these broad powers; why rely upon the fact that they will not be acted upon, in view of the fact that if they .are acted upon to the full extent very serious results may follow?

When the interpretation clause was under consideration I asked the hon. Solicitor General to give us while we were in committee a statement of the assets and liabilities of Mackenzie, Mann and Company. In the discussion of the question of default I think it is very essential that we should have that information in our possession; otherwise we shall be going along in the dark.

What the hon. gentleman asked for upon the occasion to which he refers was a statement as to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, showing their stock issue, their bond issue, the date of incorporation, the place of incorporation and their assets and liabilities. My words following his request-I have them before me and I trust the hon. gentleman will see wherein he erred yesterday in his interpretation of those words-were to the effect that there was no objection to the clause standing pending the consideration of his request and that I could see no objection to bringing down the greater part of what

he had asked for. That is the full extent of what I said.
I hope that my hon. friend made no mental reservation.

The company was incorporated in 1902; the charter is from the province of Ontario. The object of incorporation was to take over the entire assets of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and to conduct a general contracting business. The purposes of the company as set out in the charter are very wide indeed.) The bond issue is $3,000,000; the stock issue is $5,000,000. As to bringing down to the House	a statement	of all
their assets and liabilities, I do not think that that would be justified The two clauses emlbody also a power in the Governor in Council, if in his judgment Mackenzie, Mann and Company have not sufficient assets over and above liabilities to form a sufficient security, to call for other securities.	In the light of that
power vested in the Governor in Council, there is no necessity of exposing the assets or liabilities of this company to Parliament any more than the assets or liabilities of any other company.

I cannot agree with the logic of my hon. friend's statement that there is no necessity of exposing to Parliament for its information the assets and liabilities of this company any more than those of any other company. A vital and important question for us to determine is the financial condition of this company, the condition of its assets and liabilities, and whether or not it is a solvent concern and able to enter into undertakings involving millions of dollars with some expectation that the guarantee will be met. My hon. friend cannot be sincere when he undertakes to say that it is a matter of entire indifference to this committee and to Parliament what the financial position of this concern is. Any bank undertaking to finance a proposition or to go into partnership with a joint stock company, would first of all ascertain the financial position of the company. Not one of these banks whose advances are mentioned in the blue-book would deal with these parties without having a full statement of their affairs. It is equally necessary that Parliament should have full information, and I submit that the position taken by my hon. friend is the most reckless position that any Government could take in asking Parliament to ratify an agreement.
'Mr. MEIGHEN: I have only to say that I made the statement in view of the fact which the hon. gentleman overlooks in all his speeches, that if we deem, on inspection, their assets insufficient, we may call for any other contracts or undertakings that the Government may desire. In view of that, no purpose can be served by exposing: their assets and liabilities to Parliament.
Does my hon. friend' take the position that he has the statement of assets and liabilities, but declines to submit it to Parliament?
I have not said . that-

I want to emphasize that the very vital party to this agreement, comes before Parliament under the tutelage-of my hon. friend, who declines to give to Parliament or to the country any statement as to how they stand financially.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that by reason of the fact that we are bound to take their guarantee, even although we may call for others as a protection to the Crown, we should lay before Parliament a statement of the assets and liabilities, expose the private affairs of this company to Parliament? Is that his position?
I .say that these affairs have become public affairs, in virtue of the fact that the company are contracting with the Government of this country.

In 1911 the Government the hon. gentleman supported-and I say this not toy way of justification but simply toy way of comment on the earnestness and sincerity of the hon. member

took the guarantee of the Canadian Northern railway for the Canadian Northern Railway Ontario indebtedness. Did they lay before Parliament a statement of the assets and liabilities of the Canadian Northern, railway to show the value of that guarantee? There would have been some logic in doing it then because that was all the guarantee we had. But in this case we not only have the guarantee of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, but if we do not deem it sufficient on ascertaining its value, we can call for any others we wish. Where the late Government neglected to do that some case might have been made out. In this case none can be.
Mr. MACDONALD. My hon. friend cannot discuss any proposition without attempting to adopt the tu quoque argument. The
431^

lion, member for Calgary, at the very inception of the discussion of this measure, pointed out how frequently this tu quoque argument had been resorted to, by hon. gentlemen. I recall the circumstances of 1911 and I think hon. gentlemen then on this side of the House raised no question of that kind.

That does not excuse
you. Why did the hon. gentleman allow the legislation to go through if he thought that was the duty of the Government.

My hon. friend is
at the tu quoque argument again. When hon. gentlemen on both sides accept a situation, as was done in 1911 in the case of the Canadian Northern Ontario, the position is vitally different from the position to-day when a concern comes here saying that they are bankrupt.
No more than they were then.

And when hon.
gentlemen supported the proposition made by the Government, as they did in 1911, without any question, my hon. friend's tu quoque argument falls to the ground. The Liberal party in 1911 were not dealing with a concern that came here to them in extremis as this concern is now coming to the Government who say: we will not inquire for one moment as to whether the chief contracting party to this document is in a solvent financial position.

Is there not another very powerful reason why the financial standing of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited should ibe submitted to Parliament? Is it not this, that it has been announced by the Government that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are to manage the enterprise as before? So far as appears, they are to be the directors just as now; and this Government are asking the people of Canada to go into partnership with Mackenzie, Mann and Campany, Limited, in this enterprise. The undertaking has to be completed, millions of dollars have to be financed, but financed, of course, on the strength of securities which will not be availed of except as the work progresses. Have we not a right to know who the people of Canada are taking into partnership in this matter? The partnership is to be Mackenzie, Mann and Company,. Limited, and His Majesty, representing the people of Canada. Have we not a right to know7 whether our partners

are bankrupt or whether they are strong men financially and a firm or company which it is desirable that the people of Canada should be associated with in this enterprise? And yet, notwithstanding this fact, the Government refuse to give to this House any information whatever as to the financial standing of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. It does seem to me that the action of the Government is wholly inexcusable. They say: Oh we will secretly look into the affairs of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and if we think they are not able to respond to these guarantees we will take additional guarantees. Parliament is now being asked to pledge the credit of the people of this country to the exteent of $45,000,000, and surely has a right to know the financial standing of the company with which the people of Canada are to be associated in the carrying forward and completion of this undertaking.

I am afraid I do not see any additional force added to the clause by the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John. He says we are partners now

using the word very loosely as it suits hon. gentlemen opposite-consequently we should know the financial status of our partner. If that is the case, it is the duty of every party who buys a share of stock in an enterprise to ascertain the financial standing of every other stockholder in the enterprise, and a man would be very indiscreet, according to the hon. member for St. John, who bought Canadian Pacific Bailway stock before he had first gone through a book of perhaps a hundred pages to ascertain the financial standing of every other stockholder in the Canadian Pacific railway.
In this case there are only two stockholders.

The hon. member says this case is different because there are only two stockholders. Of what importance is their financial standing to us except as to their ability to run the road? In the case of the Canadian Northern agreement, which the hon. member ratified, did he expose to Parliament every asset- and every liability of the company? He never thought of it. Was not their ability to run the road of importance to him then the same as it is now? I submit that were it not for the source of this argument and the candid character of the hon. gentlman who presents it, it would be impossible for us to believe he was sincere.

There is only one conclusion to be drawn from the position of the hon. gentleman and the Government a d that is they know perfectly well that if they exposed the actual financial condition of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, it would convince the people of this country, if it did not convince this House, that it is a crime against the people of Canada not to demand that these gentlemen stand behind this guarantee and pledge their assets as security against this enormous liability of $45,000,000.

Section agreed to.
On section 22:
That upon the happening of any event of default and at any time or times while the same shall continue, it shall be lawful for the Governor in Council after such notice to the Canadian Northern as the Governor in Council may direct, to declare to be vacant the offices of the directors of the Canadian Northern and, of any of the constituent or Subsidiary companies which may be subject to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, and to appoint a board or boards of directors in lieu thereof respectively (any former director being eligible for appointment).
(a)	The power of appointment herein conferred upon the Governor In Council shall be a continuous power and shall be exercisable from time to time and so often as any event of default may exist and be continuing.

Has the Solicitor
General considered the objections which were urged by his colleague, the member for Calgary, in regard to the inadequacy of these provisions in the event of default?

The hon. gentleman
refers to the objection to a subsequent clause which provides that the Parliament of Canada may exercise the power of foreclosure. The power provided by this clause is perhaps correctly described as the power of going into possession as a receiver. The point raised by the hon. gentleman might perhaps be better discussed on a subsequent clause.

If that is a correct
statement of the effect of this section, it involves that the gentlemen who are appointed as directors by Parliament will come on the resources of the country for the purpose of running the road during the time they are in control.
I did not say that at all.

If the legal effect of section 22 is to create a receivership, the receiver cannot operate the railway or anything else without funds. If my hon. friend
calls this a receivership which gives the Government power to appoint directors, he must also agree that this section commits Parliament to the money that may be expended by those directors while they are in possession, and up to the time they come to Parliament.

The words I used were
merely by way of analogy. This is not the foreclosure clause. This is the clause that one might describe although perhaps not with the full legal effect, as the receivership clause. If we go into possession by the appointment of directors under this receivership clause, our obligations and responsibilities aTe no greater than if we go into possession under a subrogation clause which is the only remedy provided by the late Government in similar mortgages. This clause simply provides another method of going into possession.
My hon. friend agrees that it commits the country to financing the railway while its directors are in possession.

It does not commit the country to any greater extent or in any different sense than the country would be committed if it exercised the poweT of going into possession that is provided1 in the Canadian Northern Bill of 1911 or in the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill.

Section agreed to.
On section 24:
That if authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may on such terms and conditions (if any) as Parliament may prescribe, at any time while any event of default shall exist and be continuing, by order declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all persons claiming under them in the mortgaged premises to be foreclosed, and thereupon the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern (and of such other persons) in the mortgaged premises and every part thereof shall be and become absolutely barred and foreclosed, and the same shall thereupon be vested in lis Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada, any statutory enactment or any rule of law or equity to the contrary notwithstanding.

I assume that this
clause does not make it obligatory on the Government to suibmit some remedy, by way of foreclosure or otherwise, at the first session of Parliament after default; it seems to me it should be the duty of the Government of the day to do that.

Before coming to the
point raised by the hon. member for Pictou, I may say that this is the clause in respect of which consideration might be given to

the suggestion, offered by the ho-n. member a few moments ago to the effect that the power of foreclosure and taking permanent possession of the road by the people of Canada should :be automatic. From the remarks that fell from the hon. member for Pictou just now I apprehend that he himself does not give much consideration to such a suggestion.
My hon. friend has no right to draw that inference. I was only pointing out that the effect of this clause would be to suspend action indefinitely.

I was simply drawing that inference from my general estimate of the good judgment of the hon. member for Pictou, and also I think I am safe in saying that the hon. member for St. John pays no attention to such a suggestion, because, in his speech the other day, he said that, in any event, a future parliament should not be bound now to take over the property whether they wanted to or not, but that it should be left optional for Parliament to act in the premises as Parliament should deem wise. That appeals to me as so self-evident that further expatiation upon it is only a waste of time. Coming to the point which is raised by the hon. gentleman that Parliament should be compelled to act in the following session-
That the Governor in Council should submit to Parliament.
It is Parliament that * must act.
It can only do so on the initiative of the Governor in Council.

No, the Governor in Council may only do so on the initiative of Parliament. This is really the way it reads:
That if authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may on such terms and conditions (if any) as Parliament may prescribe, at any time while any event of default shall exist and be continuing, by order declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all other persons whomsoever in the mortgaged premises to be foreclosed.
If Parliament prescribes, then the Governor in Council may act.
But the Governor in Council must initiate it.

The powers given
under subsection a of section 25, while some of them may be adequate, are very wide, (and :we are making the -country responsible for the payment of securities that may be issued by these directors and giving to the Governor in Council, under a 'blank cheque, the right to eell any' securities that they can dispose of anywhere in the world and to -any amount. There is no limitation whatever.

The hon. gentleman
seems to emphasize the fact that the Governor in Council has control of the issue of securities here as he has anywhere, although I am not certain that the Governor in Council, in an ordinary case, has control at all. Is the hon. gentleman sure that an ordinary railway company has to come to the Governor in Council for power to issue bonds?
This is not a railway company after default; it is the Government operating through a. board of directors.

I know it is, hut I am under the impression, not speaking very decidedly, that a railway company, while it has to come to the Governor in Council for power to issue stock, does not have to come to the Governor in Council for power to issue bonds.
Oh, yes.

My impression is that it has not although I would not be too positive on the point. I would like the hon. gentleman to look it up and, if he does, I think he will find that I am right. In this case we are providing that the new directors, although they are the directors sf the Government, shall not issue any securities, even for the purposes of the road, unless the issue of the securities has the authorization of the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council has full control and will see to it that no issue is made beyond what is required for the legitimate purposes of the company.

That is quite true, but my hon. friend forgets that the Governor in Council is coming to Parliament now and asking permission to issue $45,000,000 while by this blanket authority we are giving by subsection a, the Governor in Council can issue securities to
any amount he wants to when these conditions arise without coming to Parliament at all. We are embarking upon the proposition of advancing $45,000,000 to these men who are now controlling this company. We are also embarking upon a proposition which involves the country, when default has arisen, in a liability to which there is no limitation except what the Government may choose to impose.

The company comes to Parliament now not for authority to issue bonds but for the guarantee of this country on the bonds. That, of course, is essential. In the other case our directors are in control of the road, running the road, and an issne of bonds secured on the road in that case would not bind the Government but it would simply bind the road.

My hon. friend would certainly be creating a very nice condition if these securities that were created by a board appointed by this Government were not securities that this country ultimately would have to pay. The good faith of this country would he absolutely and completely bound up with the action of a board which had been appointed by the Government of the day and, no matter what technicality my hon. friend may resort to for the purpose of enabling him to use the argument, ultimately the extent of the liability would be just as great as the Government of the day chose to make it without having to come to Parliament to ratify it.
There is no liability on be country whatsoever:
Does my hon. friend mean to say that the country could assume the consequences of the bad faith which would arise if they failed to stand behind its directorate?

It would be for the
Parliament of the day to decide whether it would or not, but as far as the. obligation goes, there would be no obligation resting on Parliament or the country.

What has Parliament to do with this particular section? By subsection a of section 25 the directors appointed by the Government, once default has arisen, are empowered to create an issue of securities subject only to the ratification of the Governor in Council and not of Parliament. They do not have to come back to Parliament for authority.

What I say is that the question as to whether the country would assume liability for bonds and securities so issued by these directors would be a question for the Parliament of the day to decide. There would be no obligation by virtue of this section on the Parliament of that day to decide that the country was liable for the amount of these securities.
We are simply giving a blank cheque to the Governor in Council, on default arising, to do and spend what they like.

On the security of the
road.

And Government
security too.

Subsection d of section 25 provides for the ultimate disposal of the railway system on default, and my objection to it is that this Parliament sitting to-day gives authority to a board to be created, to dispose of the system piecemeal. I am aware that the subsection contains a provision that this disposal shall be to a corporation to be created by a future parliament. It is not to my mind a satisfactory condition. Tnis is the Parliament that is providing for the guarantee, for the security, and for the conditions of default, and to my mind this is the Parliament that should provide for the ultimate disposal of the system in case of default. I am particularly interested in this feature of the case because of the branch lines of the West. In discussing this same subject with the Prime Minister on Wednesday, he assured me that, of course, it would be the intention of the Government to protect all interests that were involved in the system. I said to him then: if you will put such a provision in the resolutions, that will be satisfactory. But he not only has not done so, but to-day we are passing this section which specifically contemplates the breaking up of the system into as many pieces as may be thought suitable at the time, without any protection to those who have made themselves responsible for the financing of this system. I notice the same idea running through the communication addressed by the Prime Minister of British Columbia to the right hon. gentleman, as read in the House last night. That idea is, that this Government, having become responsible for the system should properly become responsible for the system in case of default, protecting the legitimate interests therein concerned and which are 
entitled to the protection of this House at this time. The Government of Alberta lias agreed to guarantee the bonds of the Canadian Northern and Canadian Northern Western to the extent of $21,000,000, which is a stupendous responsibility to be assumed by that province. This responsibility has been assumed by the province absolutely in the interest of the Dominion at large, and not in the interest of the provincial government, simply considered as a provincial government and considering its responsibilities as such. There was necessity for the construction of the lines that have been constructed; there is necessity for the consti lotion of the lines which are contemplated, a necessity first of all to the settlement of the country and next to the prosperity of the people who are settled there. In doing that work the provincial government did work that was national in its character and assumed a responsibility that was for the country at large. We are not asking to be relieved from that responsibility, but when this Government undertakes to assume dominant control of the whole system and becomes a partner in the enterprise, we do say that it should declare its intention and bind itself according to that declaration so that the interests of the provinces would be properly protected. Instead of that, 1 find by this section that the interests of the provinces are absolutely ignored and that it is contemplated by this Parliament that on a future occasion, default having occurred, the system may be broken up into parts. The lines which have been guaran-i teed by the provinces may be left as independent sections of transportation, under which circumstances they could not possibly be expected to meet the liabilities the provinces have guaranteed in respect of them. That is not a right provision; it i9 not a fair provision, and it is not by any means good enough to say that the parliament of a future day can take care of that situation.
We are laying heavy responsibilities upon the people of Canada; we are imposing certain conditions; we are taking dominant authority in regard to these railroads, and here and now we ought to protect the interests that are concerned, by, at any rate, saying that the Canadian Northern system shall remain a system of transportation as it was when these guarantees were given by the provinces, or, the Dominion Government should become re-

sponsible for those guarantees. That is the idea that is expressed in the telegram of the Premier of British Columbia, and I maintain it is an absolutely correct idea. In case of default, maintain the system as a separate system, give transportation and competition and allow the branches their share in the business and earnings of the system, and then the provinces have no complaint. But if you take to yourself! the right to break that system up in case of default, you should take measures to protect the interests of the provinces by assuming the guarantees they have given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend is advancing any such idea as is advanced by the Prime Minister of British Columbia; because, if I remember the correspondence correctly, the suggestion was that, because this road was made effectively a part of a great transcontinental system, the Dominion Government should take over the guarantees of the province,
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is just the converse of what the hon. gentleman suggests. These roads in Saskatchewan and Alberta to which he alludes are roads designed to serve the neighbourhoods which they traverse and to act as feeders of the Canadian Northern Railway system. They could not be put to any very useful purpose as business enterprises unless they were used as feeders to the Canadian Northern railway. Therefore, I agree with my hon. friend's suggestion from a business standpoint that it is better to keep them as part of the system, and I have no doubt that under any eventualities that course will be adopted. But it might foe possible and practicable, and desirable, that that should be accomplished through two different companies. For example, we have the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and we have the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company. They are two different corporations, but they are part of one system. It would be impracticable, I think, to make any amendment which would cover in the manner in which my hon. friend suggests the purpose which he has in view and with which I entirely agree. No Government would undertake to deal with this system in such a way as to hinder or prejudice the operation of these branch lines and feeders of the Canadian Northern Railway system and which serve the purposes of so many different communities. At the same time, I do not see that that could be provided for in advance. Further, as my hon. friend the
Solicitor General has pointed out, the only company to which any such lines could be transferred would be a company incorporated by the Parliament of Canada for that purpose. When any such proposal is placed before Parliament, if safeguards were desirable and necessary, they could be provided.

At the risk of being wearysome and of repeating what has already been said, may I go over again the view I laid before the House in this connection on Wednesday last. The fact that there is no assurance in this legislation-this legislation which takes Dominion control of these roads-that these branches will be maintained as part of the system, in the first place militates against the willingness of the provincial government to provide for their further extension, and, in the next place, militates againsit the railway company being able to secure additional funds in order to complete these necessary extensions. It is for that reason as well as for others, but for that reason especially, that it is necessary that in this legislation we should provide as to what shall be done. To again repeat myself: There is necessity for the extension of two of these lines running northeast and northwest of Edmonton, that necessity arising because of presenit actual settlement on the ground. The northeasterly line requires to be run nearly one hundred miles further than is provided for before it reaches the provincial boundary. The country is entirely settled along the north bank of the Saskatchewan river, and there are settlers there who are from fifty to one hundred miles away from railway communication at the present time, and with the Saskatchewan river intervening between them and the railway. If these people are to prosper, and if that part of the country is to progress, an extension of the railway must be provided to run one hundred miles further northeasterly from Edmonton, and it has been at a standstill for about two years. Somebody must find the money for that if it is to be done. If this Government is not to do it, the provincial Government must be expected to find the money in conjunction with the railway company. But, unless the status of that branch under all eventualities is fixed, the province will not be willing and the railway company will not be able to raise the money for the extension. A similar condition exists in regard to the northwesterly line. Provision had been

made for the construction of one hundred miles. That is practically at a standstill also. But beyond the end of this hundred miles there is a distance of two hundred miles intervening before the settlement on Grande Prairie is 4 p.m. reached. That settlement must have railway communication or it cannot stay there-at least it cannot stay there and prosper. There is an immense area of country in the Peace River district which would be affected by this road which can only be opened up and made available for settlement by the extension of this or a similar road. By this legislation as I see it, we debar the provincial Government from willingness to provide the guarantees necessary for the construction and we absolutely debar the railway company from securing the money. And yet this Government is not taking upon itself the responsibility. All I am asking at the moment is, let this Government either take the responsibility itself or let it here and now guarantee the present position of these branches in connection with the whole system for the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to want these lines left out of the system altogether ?

No, I want them kept in the system altogether. T am objecting to this provision because it contemplates the possibility of letting them out. I want a provision that will guarantee that this system shall remain a system in ease of default by the company, whereas this section provides that it may be broken up into a number of parts to the absolute detriment of these branches. My right hon. friend says that probably the Government of a future day will not break it up. Probably they will not, but that is not a sufficient guarantee to the men who are to be asked to put their money into a railway enterprise. When we have absolutely contemplated in our legislation the possibility of breaking up the system into a number of parts, I take it, men of money who are asked to invest or the provincial Government that is called upon to guarantee will hesitate and will be disinclined to make the provision necessary for this system.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is not the situation safeguarded by the fact that it must be a company incorporated by Parliament for the purpose ? They have to come to Parliament before it can be done.

I am quite aware of that, but it is a parliament of the future, and

no man can tell what a parliament of the future will do.
And you cannot bind a parliament of the future.

But you can bind this Parliament. You can make a binding arrangement to-day that will hold out to all parties concerned the fact that the intention of this Government and Parliament is to maintain this as a single railway system. But you hold out in this legislation plainly that it is not the intention to maintain :t as a single system.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend should
remember that a future Parliament may say: it was not the intention of Parliament to do that, but it ought to have done it and we are going to correct the mistake. If we strike out now the words to which my hon. friend objects, it will be perfectly open to any future parliament to put them in.
I am quite aware of that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the situation is absolutely safeguarded by the fact that before that to which my hon. friend refers can be done, Parliament must be consulted. If we leave these words out now, another Parliament may put them in; that places the matter under the control of the future parliament. Similarly, when the proposition to incorporate a company for this purpose is placed before a future Parliament, the whole question will be open: that parliament will not be bound, any more than in the case already suggested, to follow the view which may impress the Parliament of to-day.

This agreement, being
made to-day, should specifically provide what shall be done in case of the winding up of the company; it should not be left a matter for the consideration of a future Parliament. Having made certain advances, having given certain guarantees and found certain conditions existing, this Parliament should say what shall be done in case of default. This Parliament is saying that in case of default a future parliament may do as it pleases; this Parliament has no opinion on the subject. I maintain that the Parliament of to-day that is dealing with this question is the Parliament that should have an opinion. They should say under what circumstances a foreclosure shall take place and particularly

should say that that foreclosure shalll take place by the maintaining of the Canadian Northern Railway system as a separate and continuous and competitive system. They should not, on the face of the statute, hold out the suggestion that once default occurs the system may be broken up into a number of parts and the value of the branches be thereby destroyed. To my mind this is a most damaging provision. It ie not necessary. Their provisions may be made that will properly safeguard the interests of the provinces and maintain the enterprise as a united system. I would be doing much less than my duty here and now if I did not urge with all the strength of which I am capable the desirability of making siuch an amendment to these resolutions as will make that provision.

The hon. gentleman
contemplates this position. The Canadian Northern Western is to-day a provincial company and is in no way bound up with the Canadian Northern Tailway in so far as any binding mutual contract is concerned. By this legislation we do bind them together as part of one system. By the provisions for putting the directors in control, we empower those directors, if they deem it in the interests of the road, to sell, with the authority of the Parliament of Canada only, the whole or part to such a company as may be incorporated by Parliament for the purpose. Now, my hon friend says, in that way you empower the future parliament to undo the work you are doing now. He must remember that at present the Canadian Northern Western is in just the situation that he fears it may be in in the future. I acknowledge with sincere appreciation the compliment the hon. gentleman pays to the legislation which we now propose. He says that by the very union of the Canadian Northern Western, with the rest of the system, we are doing a real service to the Canadian Northern Western, to the guarantors of that road and to the people served by it. He says: so much are you doing for it and such will be the advantage to that road that I want you here and now to provide that no future parliament shall ever undo the good you are doing to-day. That is the only abjection the hon. member makes. No sale of part of the Canadian Northern Western can be made, on account of the bond issue being against it all. I can see that possibly in the future, should this road come into our hands, the sale of the Canadian Northern Western and the severance of it from the main
system might possibly be an injury to the Canadian Northern Western, to the bondholders and to the guarantors, the province of Alberta. But I do not see why we should attempt in this or in any other respect to tie the hands of a future parliament in that regard. Surely we should say that a future parliament shall be entitled to make its own mistakes. I do not think the hon. member will get the support of hon. gentlemen around him in his contention. We can scarcely conceive of a future parliament taking such action, to the detriment of a province, to the detriment of the road and against the public interest; I cannot see why this Parliament should attempt to tie the hands of a parliament ten or fifteen years hence if, perhaps under altered circumstances, they might desire to do that. In any case, it would be merely undoing what the hon. gentleman asserts to be the very good legislation which we are now putting into effect; it would be taking away from the Canadian Northern Western the benefits we give them by this legislation. All I desire to say is this: it is well to provide that if the parliament of the future finds an instance where they may sell a portion of the road to advantage and without detriment to the public or to the road, they should have the power to do so. That is all we do. I do not believe that a future parliament, any more than this, will do so if it is not for the advantage of the road and in the public interest.

The point I see in this
legislation is that in what is euphemistically called the public interest, the interest of a large section of the public is ignored. The interests I want protected are the interests of the provinces, who are the public who are directly interested in this matter.

I was commenting on the claim made toy the Solicitor General that I had said that the present legislation was putting the province of Alberta in a better position in regard to provincial guarantees of Canadian western railway lines than it would be without this legislation. I am sorry if he misunderstood me; I had no intention of expressing any such idea, and more than that I do not think such an expression would be correct. At the present time, as a business matter, the Government of Alberta is guaranteeing certain branch lines of the Canadian Northern. The province of Alberta is perfectly satisfied with the present conditions and the Canadian Northern, so far as I am aware, is satisfied with its relationship to the province of Alberta. Neither the Government of Alberta nor the Canadian Northern are asking for any legislation in that connection, and my opinion is that the position of the Government of Alberta is not bettered by this legislation. The lines of the Canadian Western are branches of the Canadian Northern lines. They are not a single system; they may be in law, but physically they are not. They leave the Canadian Northern lines at different points, they have no central terminals, and they can only exist as transportation enterprises in connection with the Canadian Northern system. Then, so long as the Canadian Northern system and the agreement between the Canadian Northern and the province of Alberta exist, the interests of the provinces are	efficiently	and sufficiently protectedwithout any such legislation as is proposed here. My hon. friend and the Prime Minister say that this legislation is not injurious and does not prejudice future action by future parliaments. If there is no prejudice and if we are to depend absolutely on a future parliament for whatever action is to be taken in this connection, then there would be no objection to striking out	this	provision altogether and	leaving the question of dealing with the railway company to a future parliament entirely.	But	the Government	doesnot	do	that.	They contemplate	and
make provision for certain action, which it is true is in a measure subject to certain action by a future parliament, but as that future parliament will consider the intent of _this_ Parliament when it passed this legislation, that will be prejudicial to the credit of this Canadian Western enterprise as regards its completion and further extension. In regard to the point I was making, I maintain that it is not only usual and right, but is quite customary and almost invariably the rule that, when such an arrangement as this is made, provision is made right in the face of the document for what shall take place in case of default. It is a well understood principle that those who take the responsibility of pledging their credit and financing an enterprise should have in mind what would be the result in case of default, and it should be shown on the face of the document.

-and that all inward and outward traffic shall be carried to Canadian ports.
And my hon. friend asks ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think this is a very mucli more effective provision than the other for the reason that, as I understand the practice, in ninety-nine per cent of the cases -or at least in a very large percentage of the cases the shipper does not pay any attention to the routing, but hands the goods over to the company to be carried

to the point of destination. Therefore, this provision is as effective, and more effective than the other. My hon. friend means to inquire whether this provision will override the ordinary rights of the shipper to fix the points of destination. I do not think that question would arise for the reason that the company is not bound under our Railway Act, so far as I am aware, to reach a point in the United States.

But does not the Prime Minister see that in the case of traffic over the Grand Trunk Pacific, if the shipper pays no attention to the routing the agreement has effect, because that agreement says that the company shall be bound to carry all out-bound traffic to a Canadian port unless otherwise routed by the shipper? But the argument has been made, and now my right hon. friend himself says that this section is more effective. I am not able to see that. This is what I want to know: Suppose a shipper in Winnipeg wants to send, say, a thousand barrels of flour to Liverpool, and directs that it shall be routed via Montreal and Portland, there to take the steamer for Liverpool-perhaps he may get a lower rate which may induce him to choose that route -is it intended by this clause to prevent the Canadian Northern railway from taking that shipment of flour in accordance with the orders of the shipper?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as the rate is concerned, there is an express provision not only in this statute but in the statute passed in 1903-4 respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific, that the rate via Canadian ports shall not be higher than via American ports. Therefore, the premise he mentions could not exist. As to the other point, I am not aware that there is any obligation upon our railway companies under our Railway Act to carry goods in that way. I mean, I do not know that there is any common law or other right of the shipper in this country to insist upon that. At all events, whether that is the case or not, I say this provision will be effective, because as I understand the methods of shipping, it is left, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, to the railway company itself-and perhaps I am stating it at too low a percentage-
Does the hon. gentleman mean the proportion of cases of routing by the shipper?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I say, I am told by shippers that in ninety-nine per cent of the cases they give their goods to the railway

company, stating the destination but leaving the routing to the railway.
Not ninety-nine out of a hundred cases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

Very frequently we state definitely how we want the goods routed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think that the
question which my hon. friend raises has any particular import.
If in 99 oases out of 100, as my right hon. friend says, the shipper pays no attention to routing, is not the Grand Trunk Pacific agreement just as effective as this agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think so.
Why?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because the burden is
cast most distinctly upon the railway company in this case. If it should be possible for the shipper to direct the routing, they make a distinct, specific and absolute engagement that the goods shall be carried over lines in Canada and via Canadian ports. It will be very much more easy to detect any attempt to violate that provision, than it would under the former provision, as I apprehend it

I do not see why, because in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific there is an absolute and express obligation to carry all goods for foreign shipment through Canadian ports unless otherwise routed and the obligation would: be on the Grand Trunk Pacific to show that the directions of the shipper were otherwise. I do not think there would be any difference in that respect; what I want to know is whether it is the opinion of my right hon. friend that the effect of this legislation, if it goes through, will be to compel the Canadian Northern Railway Company to carry all traffic originating on its system and destined, we will say, for Liverpool, through Canadian ports and refuse to hand it over to a railway company at Montreal or any other place for the purpose of taking it through an American port, even although 2731
the shipper has ordered it to be taken out via an American port.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not at all convinced that any railway company in this' country is compellable to route traffic in the way my hon. friend suggests. Whether that be the case or not, we have thought it desirable that there should be this absolute and distinct provision that goods shall be carried by Canadian lines and through Canadian ports. The marked difference between this case and the case to which my hon. friend alludes, that of the Grand Trunk Pacific, is this: that in that case there were, in name and in form, two corporations, while there was but one corporation in interest. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, having very large interests in Poruand and controlling absolutely the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, could, through its canvassers and agents, bring about a specific routing by the shipper which would not otherwise be made. The provision made in that case, therefore, might, and perhaps would, in the end result in absolute disappointment in respect of the expectations which were based upon it.

The first part of this clause says:
That at all times hereafter all freight originating on the lines of the Canadian Northern or on the lines of any of the constituent companies, or on any line or lines of railway now or hereafter owned, leased or operated by the Canadian Northern or by any of the constituent or subsidiary companies, their successors or assigns, shall, when destined to points in Canada, be carried over the lines of the Canadian Northern or over some other Canadian railway or railways.
If I wanted to send articles to someplace in the West where both the American; lines and the Canadian Northern line operated, and my consignee wanted it sent by the Hill lines, the Canadian Northern would lose the freight; there is no doubt about that, because I would send it whichever way my consignee wanted it sent. For that reason I think the Canadian Northern would be out of pocket in respect of this loss of freight. Iln the latter part of the clause it is said that the Canadian Northern and several constituent and subsidiary companies shall not in any manner within their power or control directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of any such freight by routes other than those above provided. That seems reasonable enough, but I think that, under the first part of the clause, you are

putting them in a position where they will lose freight.
iMr. PUGSLEY: It is provided here that *all inward ocean traffic shall be carried to Canadian ports. What does that mean? Does it mean that if inward traffic comes to Portland and goes over the rails to Montreal, destined for points on the Canadian Northern, the 'Canadian Northern shall not be allowed to carry it to its proposed destination because it has not come through a Canadian port? Surely that means that the Canadian Northern is prohibited from carrying any traffic over its lines that has not come through a Canadian port, else how is it to be enforced?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: One of the constituent companies is a steamship company.

I know it is, but that
steamship line does not carry all the inward ocean freight. There has been so much delay in bringing intt^ effect the provisions of the Act of Parliament passed when the late Government was in power, providing that the British preference should apply only to goods brought direct to Canadian ports, that a good deal of traffic destined for Canadian points goes to Portland. Under this clause, about which there has been so much boasting in this House and in the newspapers, it is provided that all inward ocean freight over the Canadian Northern shall be brought to Canadian ports. Does not that mean that if goods come to Portland destined to points on tne Canadian Northern, the Canadian Northern railway must refuse to receive that freight and that if they do not refuse it, they are disobeying the provisions of the statute? Under the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific it was provided ' unless otherwise routed ', but here is the positive legislative prohibition that they must not carry any goods destined for outward voyage except through Canadian ports and that they must not carry any inward traffic except that which comes to Canadian p-orts. My own judgment is that you cannot enforce this provision; you are proposing to put in tl>e statute a provision simply in order that you may make the boast that you have done something better than the ' late Government did in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. You have not the remotest idea that it will be productive of any good or that it will ever be enforced. Let the Government say whether it is intended to prohibit any goods being carried over the Canadian Northern, if for 
foreign shipment, unless they are destined to go through Canadian ports. Let it be declared that it is the intention of the Government absolutely to prohibit the Canadian Northern railway from accepting or carrying any traffic that comes to Canada otherwise than through Canadian ports and let penalties be provided; then the Government will show that they are sincere. It does seem to me that at the present time the Government are open to the charge of having done something with a mere pretence of accomplishing something which the late Government were not able to accomplish under their agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and that they are really providing no effective mean3 of carrying out the provisions made in that regard.

I wish to bring forward
another feature of the freight rates question in connection with clause a. Clause a undertakes to declare that there shall be equality of freight rates over unequal distances. All I wish to ask is that there shall be a declaration that there shall be equal freight rates over equal distances under equal conditions. Once the Government undertake to say, as they do in this subsection, that they have the right to require railway companies to carry traffic over longer routes at the same rates as are charged over shorter routes, they cannot refuse fairly to accept the proposal that I desire to bring to their attention. It is within the knowledge of the Government and of the House that there is an inequality of freight rates levied by the railway com panies as between eastern and western Canada. The same railway companies operating in eastern Canada charge lower local freight rates than they do in western Canada. This has been a grievance in western Canada for some years. It has been ventilated very fully in the press and in this House; dt has been brought to the attention of the Railway Commission; the Railway Commission have given a decision which, so far as a decision of the rtailway Commission could, established and confirmed the principle of inequality in freight rates between eastern and western Canada. This decision of the Railway Commission was a very great disappointment to the people of western Canada and is considered by them to constitute a very grave injustice upon them, in fact to be a miscarriage of justice at the hands of tne Railway Commission. The Board of Trade of the city of Winnipeg passed a
MA\ 27, 1914
4329'
resolution on this subject which I shall read. It was passed on May 12, 1914:
Whereas, the Winnipeg Board of Trade petitioned the Government of Canada, under date of November 14, 1911, to, by legislation la* down the principle that rates charged by railways in western Canada should not exceed those charged in eastern Canada for similar service, to a greater extent than necessary to cover additional cost of performing the service, if any, in western Canada ; and
Whereas, the Government of Canada caused an investigation to be made by the Board ot Railway Commissioners into the rates charged by railways for carriage of freight in western Canada; and
Whereas, the Board of Railway Commissioners has held repeated hearings, taken voluminous evidence from the many interests involved, and, after consideration thereof, has given its decision; and
Whereas, by its judgment, dated April 6, 1914, the Board of Railway Commissioners has declined to grant western Canada that equality of treatment with eastern Canada in the matter of freight rates which has been advocated by the Winnipeg Board of Trade for many years past, but has simply ordered reductions in certain rates; and
Whereas, the Board of Railway Commissioners in its said judgment holds that the Railway Act permits discrimination between localities under certain conditions;
Therefore be it resolved, that while the Winnipeg Board of Trade welcomes the reductions ordered by the Board of Railway Commissioners, which slightly lessen the disparity between freight rates charged in eastern and western Canada, this board emphatically protests against the discrimination which still remains between rates ordered by the commissioners for the carriage of freight in western Canada and the rates charged for similar service in eastern Canada; and
Be it further resolved, that the Winnipeg Board of Trade reiterates the position it has always taken, viz., that no basis of freight rates will be fair, just and equitable to the people of western Canada which permits of higher rates being charged for the carriage of freight in western Canada than is charged for like service in eastern Canada (except in so far as cost of performing the service may be greater), and this board respectfully urges the Government of Canada to effect such a change in the Railway Act, when the present contemplated revision of the Act is made, as will embody the principle of equality which this board has always advocated and maintained.
By order of the president,
Tours truly,
C. N. Bell,
Secretary.
We are to-day making an arrangement with a great railway system which operates in both eastern and in western Canada, and the purpose of the aid that we propose to give is to further confirm and establish that railway system as a system of transportation throughout Canada from ocean to ocean, both in East and West. Under the conditions as set forth by the Winnipeg Board of Trade, and in view of the decision taken by the Government in this subsection as to their
right to require discriminating freight rates at the hands of the Canadian Northern railway, I maintain that there is no other just,. fair or reasonable course open to this Parliament than to require that equalized freight rates shall prevail throughout this Canadian Northern Railway system, this transconti-ental railway system operating in eastern and in western Canada.
Would the hon. gentleman say just where in clause a that is discriminated against, what clause in the agreement prevents equality of freight rates?

It is the provision which requires the company to carry to Canadian ocean ports at the same rates as to American ocean ports, without regard to the fact that the distances are greater to Canadian than to American ocean ports.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I am not asking the Government to make a rate requiring the company to discriminate in regard to western business; all I am asking the Government to do is to apply the terms of these resolutions to western Canada, and require-an equalization of freight rates, as they have required discrimination in freight rates in favour of certain sections of eastern Canada. Provided always that every agreement re-, specting the interchange of traffic shall be subject to any agreements now existing with any other company or companies.
A few days ago I brought this matter to the attention of the House, and the Solicitor Generali said:	Oh, that cannot apply,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Might I interrupt my
right hon. friend to tell him what the clause was intended to mean and what, I think, it does mean. The clause deals with mutual interchange of traffic between

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:

Every agreement respecting the interchange of traffic shall be subject to any agreements now existing with any other company or companies.
-not with any Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I desire to give the most respectful consideration to my right hon. friend's objection. I am only pointing out the language of the clause. 'friend suggests. Council.

In	a	long	distance a company	would	not	take
running rights unless it also_can have the right to pick up local traffic. I would ask my right hon. friend if he does not think it would be desirable that the words ' and as may be approved by the Governor in Council,' should be added.

speechtext: The suggestion otf my hon. friend is entitled to consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:

INTERPRETATION CLAUSES:
* Constituent companies ' means such of those companies mentioned in the first schedule to the following resolutions, and such other companies hereafter declared by the Governor in Council to be comprised in the Canadian Northern system, as own or operate railways, terminals, bridges or other railway facilities.
1 Subsidiary companies ' means such of those companies mention^ in said schedule, and such other companies, hereafter declared by the Governor in Council to be comprised in the Canadian Northern system, as do not own or operate railways, terminals, bridges or other railway facilities.

Some doubt was expressed when the matter came up as to whether or not the Government had in their minds any line which they thought likely to be declared under the provisions of this interpretation clause to be included in the Canadian Northern Railway system. It seems to me that some fuller definition of the object and purport of the definition should be given. Otherwise the Governor in Council could declare any railway in Canada a part of the Canadian Northern railway. It is intended to include railways which are at present owned by the contractors or in which they are interested in some way which might hereafter be declared to be part of the system?
The hon. gentleman asks either gs to what it is the intention to declare or as to what is the power given, I am not sure which-perhaps it was both. '
Both.

As to intention, there is no present intention concerning any particular line or class of lines. The power is general, as the hon. gentleman states; the Governor in Council has power to add to the system any time. It would necessarily be on the application of the company, and the Governor in Council would have to be satisfied that the addition was in the interest of the company itself, and, of course, impliedly, would be empowered to stipulate the terms on which it should be declared a part of the system.

Does the hon. gentleman think the language should be so general as to include any railway in Canada? Even though it might not reasonably form part of a transcontinental railway? The declared object of these resolutions as given in the recitals, and the basis on which the Government seeks justification for entering into this partnership, is the completion of
4.334

a third transcontinental line. There maybe lines that by no possibility of theory could form part of this transcontinental system. Is it intended that the powers should be so great that you could bring in lines from outside the system altogether?

So far as the power is concerned, I think that is a necessity. I do not think there would 'be any possibility of another definition thaWwould be workable at all. I think the Governor in Council would never approve of the addition of a company nor -would the company itself apply for inclusion if its road physically or in the nature of things in the railway world were completely aside from this system. At the same time, there would! be no use in inserting such expression as 'naturally a part of the system,' for -the words would be so indefinite as to be ineffective. At the same time there would ibe no great purpose to be served by such an expression because the Governor in Council has full control. And it seems to be one of those classes of cases where it is necessary that there should be such control .and that we should rely upon it.

Do I understand

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

On section 6-commencement of Act:

Is the minister
aware that the price of nails has been increased by some 25 cents per keg since the change in the tariff on steel wire has come into effect? I rather understood him to intimate that there was some arrangement between the Government andi the trade whereby this (was not likely to occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The increase in the price of nails is not due to any tariff change in regard to wire rods. The duty has not been changed on nails, it remains at 60 cents a keg.
The duty on wire rods has.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The price of nails is governed, like the price of any other commodity by supply and demand.
The tariff has nothing to do with this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not changed1 the
tariff.

You did change the
tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as foreign nail manufacturers are competitors in the Canadian market, the duty upon nails might have a bearing upon the price of nails; but, as I stated, we have not changed the tariff upon nails. Presumably, therefore, the nail makers obtain such prices as they are able to obtain for their product. They would do that before the tariff change was made on wire rods. They are doing that, no doubt, to-day. They are obtaining for their commodity the price which it commands in the
market of Canada. The price of nails has greatly fallen during the last year or year and a half. I would expect that by reason of the falling off in the building trade. There is no doubt an improvement in that regard and that improvement, I hope, will be more marked in the near future. The result will be that the price of nails may go up. Whether it has gone up or not I do not know. I take the word of my hon. friend that that has happened, but I would point out that we have not touched the tariff upon nails.

We have touched the
tariff on the raw material that goes into the manufacture of nails. On Monday last I met the principal hardware merchant of Woodstock who told me that, as a result of the change in the tariff, he is paying 25 cents a keg more for nails than two months ago and will have to continue to do so. The wholesaler tells him that he is compelled to charge the 25 cents extra because the tariff increases the price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why did the price of nails go down much more than 25 cents a keg in the last year and a half without any tariff change at all?

I do not know that; I
only know that, as a result of a change in the tariff, the price has gone up 25 cents.
