I think I can suggest to the minister why the price went down. Some few years ago there was a combine between the nail makers and they made a price to the trade. That combine fell through to some extent, and as a result nails went down to their market value. I have no doubt that competition is very keen, and perhaps there was not a legitimate profit in the business; but I venture to assert, what I conjectured before, that nails would advance in price because of the change in duty on rods. That would not be so bad, but as I explained to the committee on a previous occasion, there is, to all intents and purposes, a combine by which the price of nails is fixed, as the price is now in the hands of two of the largp nail makers. These nail makers are the makers of the rods; they make the price for the rods to the small nail makers and make the price of nails to the trade at large. It is an easy matter for them to control the price so long as you keep the duty of sixty cents a keg on nails. There is not a question in my mind but as a result of the increased duty on rods there has been an advance in the price of nails; and there will be a still further advance

because the retail men must have a profit on this extra twenty-five cents that the wholesale men pay. I venture to assert, as I did before, that in the end the result will be that the consuming public of Canada will pay each year $750,000 extra owing to the increased cost of nails. We produce in Canada about one and a half million kegs of nails in twelve months, and the consuming public, in my judgment, will, in the future, because of this arrangement made with the two rod rolling mills in Canada, pay practically fifty cents per keg as an extra price on wire nails.
Would the minister explain subsection 2 of section 2 of the Bill, and also sections 3 and 4.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Subsection 2 of section 2 reads:
Goods the product or manufacture of any foreign country imported into Canada in vessels admitted to registration under the laws of such foreign country may, if such foreign country imposes higher duties of customs upon goods imported into such country in vessels registered in Canada than upon the like goods when imported in vessels of such country, be made subject by order of the Governor in Council in the case of goods already dutiable to a surtax over and above the duties specified in schedule A to this Act, and in the case of goods not dutiable to a rate duty, not exceeding, in either case, twenty per centum ad valorem.
It appears to me that the meaning of the subsection is perfectly clear.
Where a foreign country -imposes higher duties upon- goods the product or manufacture of Canada imported in Canadian vessels than upon such goods when imported into such foreign countries in their own vossels, the Governor -in Council may impose a surtax over and -above the duties of our customs tariff upon the goods of such nation to an amount not exceeding 20 per cent ad valorem: it may be 5, 10 or 15 per cent, but must not exceed 20 per cent. The subsection applies in the case -of both dutiable and free goods and is to cover the case of discrimination against Canadian vessels.

In the United
States tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That may be a case in
point, bnt the legislation is general. It is not in my mind that we shall have occasion to enforce it. As I -stated when this section was under discussion before, the Government would be exceedingly reluctant to impose -a surtax unless compelled

to such a course obviously and deadly in the public interest.

I was under the impression, from what my hon. friend is reported to have said, that this Government would not frame its tariff in any way with reference to the tariff of another country. I read a report of -some remarks of the hon. gentleman about putting wheat on the free list, the result of w-hich would be to enable the farmers of Canada, particularly of the West, to get a free market in the United States for their wheat; and it was in that connection that the hon. gentleman was reported- to have said that this Government was not going to frame its tariff having any reference to the tariff of another eonntry. If that is so, why should Parliament give power to impose a surtax because some otheT country has framed its tariff in a particular way? It seems to me the same rule ought to apply in both cases. Does it not show, notwithstanding what may be -the feeling of my hon. friend, that he recognize-s that in the public interest Canada must have regard to the tariffs of other countries? Any prudent Government would -recognize that fact. While I do not want to take up the time of the committee, I want to take this opportunity-the first I have had this- session, unfortunately-of expressing my deep regret that the Government has not seen fit to place certain imported food products, more especially wheat, on the -free list. The Government ought not to forget that the United States has passed a tariff law under which it is provided that if any other country -should place wheat and wheat products upon the free list, wheat and wheat products would be admitted into the United States free of duty. I know something about our western country. I have had business relations with many people in the Northwest extending over a period of more than a quarter of a century. I know a good deal of the condition of affairs in our western country, and! I know that since it was announced that it was the settled determination of this Government not to place wheat upon the free list a feeling of despair, almost, was created in western Canada. The people had hoped that the Government would take a reasonable view of this question, and that they would welcome the opportunity of giving to our farmers free access to the great American market to the south;

but they have been greatly disappointed, and I have no doubt that the deplorable falling off in immigration from the United, States into western Canada is to a large' extent the result of the feeling which has been brought about in the West by reason of the action of the Government in refusing the request of the western farmers. I thought it due to myself that I should take this opportunity of expressing the very deep regret I feel in common with hundreds of thousands of the people of this country that this Government has not availed itself of the splendid opportunity which has been afforded by the legislation of the United^ States to obtain enlarged markets for the wheat produced by the farmers of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not desire to re-open the Budget discussion, but I may say to my hon. friend that he no doubt refers to a statement which I made in my Budget speech when dealing with wheat and flour.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have ' Hansard ' in my hand, and what I said was this:
Speaking generally, it is not advisable that a nation's tariff should be so arranged as to fit into the particular features of that of another nation. This, however, would not he a conclusive reason for not making a change clearly in the national interest.
That is slightly different from what my hon. friend stated that I said:
I stated that you were re. ported to have said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In regard to the particular section now under discussion, I should like to point out that the legislation is not directed against any particular nation. It is not a fitting of our tariff into the special features of another country's tariff. The legislation is general. It merely provides [DOT]that the Governor in Council may impose a surtax upon goods the product or manufacture of another country which discriminates against Canada by imposing higher rates of duty upon goods carried in Canadian vessels.

Why has the minister
changed the provisions of the present section 7? Under the present Tariff Act, the surtax is absolutely fixed by Parliament at one-third of the general tariff. By the new Tariff Act, it is provided that the minister has the right to fix this surtax, excepting subsection 2 which provides for the surtax imposed upon goods going into the United States in any but United States
vessels. What is the reason for changing it from the positive Act of Parliament to the discretion of the minister? Does it not leave the matter open for the minister to make one trade with one importer and another trade with another? Does it not leave the matter open to lobbying between the importers and the minister? I think the minister should give some reason for changing an Act of Parliament into an Order in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I direct my hon. friend's attention to section 7 of the present Customs tariff:
Articles which are the produce or manufacture of any foreign country which treats imports from Canada less favourably than those from other countries may he subject to a surtax over and above the duties specified in schedule A to this Act, such surtax in every case to be one-third of the duty specified in the general tariff in the said schedule.
Any question arising as to any foreign country or goods coming under the operation of this section shall be decided by the Minister of Customs, whose decision shall be final.
The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this section, and may, by Order in Council, from time to time suspend the surtax from application to the goods of any country.
So power is given to the Governor in Council. Subsection 1 of section 2 of the Bill now under consideration provides that the Governor in Council may impose a surtax over and above the regular duties to an amount not exceeding twenty per cent ad valorem.	The difference between the two	sections is	this.
Under the present tariff the amount of the surtax is fixed at 33J per cent which is a very heavy surtax. Take the case of goods dutiable at 35 per cent; one-third of 35 per cent would be nearly 12 per cent. There is no power to change that. It may appear desirable to the Government to impose a surtax of 2 per cent or 5 per cent, but not one of 12 per cent. The tariff rate might be too high; it might be prohibitive, with the surtax of 33J per cent imposed on the goods sought to be imported; it might be so high that it would be prohibitive if such a rate of duty by way of surtax were.imposed. The amount of the surtax will be left to the discretion of the Governor in Council.

That is just the objection. If there be a surtax it is imposed for a purpose; it is a penalty. I object to the degree of the penalty being left in the discretion of the minister. I think that if there is to be a penalty Parliament should impose it and not the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Governor in. Council.

Under the present law
the only power the Governor in Council has is to withdraw it entirely.
Is it not a provision against outside dumping.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a provision against dumping; it is a provision in keeping with the legislation passed under the former Government for protecting the people of Canada against discrimination by foreign countries. The legislation is general and not aimed at any particular nation.

That is a right we take to impose a penalty against any foreign country treating us unfairly. All foreign countries have notice that if they want to do business with Canada they must treat us the same as they treat other nations or we will impose a surtax of one-third of our tariff against goods coming from that country into Canada. If it. has any value at all it is a notice to the world. Now ail that is taken away by the Government and foreign countries will say there is nothing rigid about it as far as Canada is concerned and we can treat them unfairly if we wish. Then it is up to our importers to come to Ottawa and make the best trade they can with the Government. You are taking away all the benefit of the surtax. It is now placed in the position where each individual importer can come to the Government and make whatever trade is possible. The present law is a notice to foreign countries that if they do not treat Canada fairly in tariff matters their producers who want to sell goods in Canada will be compelled to pay a fixed penalty.

It is really a
provision for retaliation?
Yes, that is what it is.

I do not believe in these silly provisions at all, but if you are going to retaliate it would be a good thing to be able to do it quickly, and the Governor in Council can act very much more quickly than can Parliament.

But the present law hits quickly now; Parliament says that the surtax shall be one-third and every person knows what it is. This Bill places the minister in a position to dicker with the importer. The importer comes here and says one-third is too much, will you not make it 15 per cent? The minister cuts it down to fifteen and the importer says that is too

much, cut it down to 10. In all probability, if-he has sufficient influence, he will get it cut down to nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend knows that this is general legislation and that we will not be ' dickering ' with any importer.

I would like to direct the attention of the minister to schedule c-prohibited goods. There are added to the list of prohibited goods certain articles of apparel. Is it the intention that this provision shall be enforced with respect to those articles of apparel when they are in use as articles of apparel, or is it only to be applied in cases of their importation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is intended to apply to their importation. Schedule c of the present Customs Tariff contains a list of prohibited goods. If my hon. friend will turn to section 11 of the Customs Tariff of 1907, he will find the following:
The importation into Canada of any goods enumerated, described or referred to in schedule ' C ' to this Act is prohibited ; and any such goods imported shall thereby become forfeited to the Crown and shall be destroyed or otherwise dealt with as the Minister of Customs directs; and any person importing any such prohibited goods, or causing or permitting them to be imported, shall for each offence incur a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars.
The section refers to the importation of goods, not to goods in the country, and we are adding to the list the articles enumerated on page 9 of the Bill, to which my hon. friend drew my attention.

There is a provision in the tariff that wearing apparel is not dutiable. If these articles come in as wearing apparel in use is it the intention of the Government to prohibit their coming in? Do the Government propose following the example of our neighbours to the south of the line in making this prohibition? I want to know if they are going to follow their example in the administration of the prohibition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As the statute is worded, undoubtedly, the Customs Department would enforce it as against parties wearing these plumes and other articles mentioned. The intention of this legislation is to prevent the destruction of these birds. My hon. friend may know that they are being destroyed, and destroyed with great cruelty. Not only has the United States prohibited the importation of these ^plumes, feathers and other parts of birds, but the Commonwealth of Australia has done likewise.

Similar legislation was introduced into the British House of Commons on the 13th of February last, and on March 7 the Bill was reported and received its second reading. I should say that the statute would apply to plumes if worn by the parties bringing them into the country.

I am not going to question the advisability of these articles being added to the list of prohibited goods, but I certainly wish to take this opportunity of protesting against the administration of this provision as I am credibly informed it has been enforced by the United States customs officials. I think that it is an atrocity to subject ladies to insult at the hands of customs officials, in depriving them of articles of ornament which they have become possessed of as a matter of right and under the law of whatever country they were in. I am quite willing to be a party to assisting in the protection of the birds affected, but I think that the protection and preservation of the self-respect of lady travellers, either Canadian or of other countries visiting Canada, as well as the selfrespect of this Dominion, is just as important as the protection of the birds. I must protest very strongly against the -administration of this provision as it has been administered south of the line, where it has been used as a means of insult, which I hope will not be followed in Canada. If we cannot have a law that can be administered without unnecessarily insulting people, we had better let the law go and let somebody else take this matter in hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The apprehensions of my
hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) are not well founded. I should hope that the customs officials of Canada axe gentlemen, and that they will under no circumstances offer insult to anybody. I shall be glad to look into the matter and see if we can obviate any disagreeable results so far as inconvenience to the travelling public is concerned. I am in sympathy with my hon. friend with regard to his observations on the administration of the Act, but I think it is very desirable legislation.

If you amend the law so as to except articles actually in use as part of wearing apparel, it would remove any possibility of unfortunate administration. I would be sorry to have this law administered in the Dominion as T am credibly informed it is administered in the United States, and I trust the minister will not leave this section in such shape that an indiscreet
customs official might impose undue humiliation upon ladies who are travelling.

If subsection c were
eliminated it might make the law more drastic, but it would make it easier to administer. The law allows the wearing of the feather of a bird which is ordinarily used as an article of diet, and if a lady who comes from South Africa or from Australia is wearing the plumage of some bird that is used there as an article of diet, but which the customs official does not know as such, he no doubt would proceed to eliminate that feather from her hat by taking out his jackknife and cutting it off. I am pointing out the ridiculous side of this to show the minister what trouble it may lead to.
Mr. LOGGI.E: I am informed that it is not now contemplated to enforce a law similar to this in the United
9 p.m. Kingdom, as it has been found not to be practicable. That may also be the case in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is advisable that the section should stand as it is, and we shall see how it works out. I do not anticipate that trouble which hon. gentlemen opposite apprehend, but if there should be, there will be time enough to amend the Act.
Mr. LOGGiIE: The only manufacturer of feathers in Canada told me recently that he is very much opposed to this legislation. Whether he was speaking from a selfish standpoint or not I cannot say. I suggested that the best thing for him to do would be to place the ease personally before the Commissioner of Customs and the Minister of Finance, and I understand he contemplates doing so. He told me they had abandoned the idea of enforcing this law in the United Kingdom, as they found it impracticable.
Bill reported.

On motion of Hon. Sam Hughes, Bill No. 176, to make further provision for bounties to volunteers who served the Crown during the Fenian raids, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Would the minister explain the difference between this and the legislation now on the statute-books?

There is really no change; it is an extension oi the present law. Originally this Bill was for one year, but the officers inform me that we shall not be able to get all the warrants out in time, and I would suggest that sections 3 and 4 be amended by substituting for the words '31st December, 1914' the words, '1st July, 1915.' Under the former Bill it was payable directly to the volunteer; but in cases where the volunteer was dead there was often great trouble in getting his propertv probated. This takes the precaution of making it payable to his widow.
Why is the bounty limited' to the case of the volunteer who was living on the 1st of April, 1912? If he happened to die before that, why should not his widow get the bounty?
That was in the old Act. We are modelling the new Bill on the old.

I asked the minister some time ago, in connection with this Bill, if provision was made for the case of the force raised in Manitoba in 1871 or 1872 to repel the raid by O'Neill at Pembina? I understand that that force is excluded from the benefits of the Act. I wish to renew the inquiry and ask whether the men of this force would be eligible under this Act.

The hon. member will
see that under section 2 it is confined to those who were called out for active service in 1866 or 1870. The original Bill read that way.

But why should these
volunteers who actually took part in repelling a raid be excluded from benefiting by the Bill?
I am merely renewing an old Bill. I have no data as to the calling out of the troops at the time to which the hon. gentleman refers.' We thought we had covered everything.

I wish to call the minister's attention to the fact that such troops were raised for active service and to repel an actual raid. It seems to me absurd and most unjust that while thousands of men who were called upon for service during the Fenian excitement in other provinces receive recognition these men who, under very extraordinary circumstances, actually took part in yrhat might be called a campaign should be ignored by the terms of the Bill. It never struck me, when the Bill came up first, that there could be such a condition.

I did not pay as much attention to it, probably, as I should have done. But having failed heretofore, I want it to be understood that I do not fail now. There was such a raid, there was such a service, and I make claim on 'behalf of these men for recognition under the terms of the Bill.

Did these men actually take part in that campaign ? I have men in my county who were in this force, and I have asked them to make their claim. But the only claim I have had set up for these men was that they were under arms for eight or ten days. I do not think they were in active service.

There was no actual bloodshed, but O'Neill crossed the boundary at Pembina and took possession of West Lyhne, keeping his base of operations still in Pembina. The American officer in command there took such measures as prevented a permanent occupation of West Lynne by the invading force; but while this was in progress a volunteer force was raised in Winnipeg, and that force marched to Pembina, or towards Pembina. They were actually under arms and in active service, and, so far as their idea of it was concerned, they felt themselves to be simply an outpost of British authority, without backing, for they had no reserve behind them.
They were real heroes.

They were. They did not know but this might be an invasion in force. I think that if any men in Canada are entitled to consideration, these are the men; for, not caring what the force of men in front of them was, and, without any support behind them, they turned out at the first call and did what they conceived to be their duty; and I believe that what they did had just as much effect in breaking the raid as had the action of the United States authorities.
How many men were there ?

I do not recollect; it was not a large force; but the men forming that force did not know what force might be against them. They turned out to repel an armed attack upon the soil of Canada. They did not know what was behind O'Neill, but they turned out regardless of that; and I believe that the fact that they turned out as promptly as they did had a great deal more to do with breaking the raid than the fact that the American officer took charge

of O'Neill's men. Had there been no pretence of force in Winnipeg, I am afraid the United States authority would not have seen his duty and done it as quickly as he did.

I want to point out to
the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) that he has been remiss in his duty. There is no doulbt that his constituents actually did turn out to repel an invasion of Canada. The minister has given some ten or twelve thousand men in Nova Scotia this $100, though all they did was to be in Nova Scotia when some loyal old governor issued a proclamation calling upon them to turn out. There was no invasion of .Nova Scotia, and no threateened invasion; but the governor in a fit of patriotism thought it necessary to issue a proclamation calling upon every able-bodied man in the province, as I recollect it, from eighteen to forty-five years of age. Some of them came out, I presume, and some of them did not, but they are all getting the $100. Now, my hon. friend from Selkirk has really a grievance against the minister, foT, if I may -believe the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), here were real heroes defending the country, men entitled to this $100. I think the minister should have his attention called to the matter very forcibly, and these men should be recognized.

I shall be glad to look into the facts in regard to the raid in Manitoba. We have no date in the department bearing on the subject to justify action. If it is found by next session that there is any justification for taking the Manitoba division into consideration, so far as I am concerned I shall be only too glad to bring in another Bill.
I do not think that is fair at all. This man O'Neill was the leader at Ridgeway; I am not sure that he was not the leader at another raid in the Eastern Townships.
Was he not a brother?

I do not know his relation, ship, but I know that the name is the same, and I understand that it was the same man. It never struck me for a moment when I saw the Bill in the first place that these men were not included; I was never satisfied that they were not included until I asked the minister across the floor of the House some time during this session. I think the minister would do himself credit if he would hold the Bill over until he could frame an amendment' that would 274
take these men in. There is no -question about the facts; there is no question about the raid or about the service rendered. The only question is as to who took part in the service and who are personally entitled to the bounty. Every member representing a Manitoba constituency, if not of his own knowledge, certainly on the evidence of people who are absolutely reliable, and who know the facts, can inform the minister, as I have done, that this service was rendered and that it is absolutely well worthy of recognition.

Were these men in regular companies, or were they simply volunteers?
. Mr. OLIVER: They were volunteers. I was not i-n Manitoba at the time, but the event was very fresh in the minds of the people when I went there in 1873. As I understand it, these men were enlisted on the authority of the then lieutenant governor of the province. Volunteers were called; these men volunteered; they were properly enrolled for active service and, so far as my knowledge goes, everything was regularly done and must be of record in the Militia Department.

In the county adjoining
mine, the county of Lincoln, there is- a striking case where the men who belonged to a certain company have a grievance. At the time of the Fenian raid, which took place in the neighbourhood of my own county, different battalions in that district were called out to active service. Either the 19th or the 44th Regiment of the county of Lincoln, which were called out at that time, formed an extra company; that is, they added a company of volunteers; to their battalion when they went to the front. That company was furnished with all the necessary ammunition, uniforms, guns and things of that sort and actually went to the front at Ridgeway; they engaged in active service with the Fenians at the time they landed in Canada. Through neglect on the part of the captain of the company that was formed at the time, they were never, properly registered at Ottawa. I have taken this matter up with the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), who we all regret is not with us to-night, and I understand that some twelve or fourteen men belonging to that company engaged in actual service. I believe the Government should recognize their services and that they should receive) the bounty. One of the men, a resident of my town, and a most reputable man.

434?

gives me this information. I think that the neglect of the captain of their company hi not registering their names at Ottawa does not alter the fact that they are justi as much enitled to the bounty as men who have been members of a properly registered company.

I shall be interested to hear what answer my hon. friend the minister will make to the case just presented by the hon. member for Haldimand. When this matter was before the House for discussion on a previous occasion the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) called the attention of the House to the case of a regiment from his locality which participated in the Fenian raid. The minister stated that for some reason or other they were not entitled to the Fenian raid bounty. I have never been able to understand upon what principle the minister can justify his refusal to pay the bounty to these men. Surely the purpose of the bounty is to reward the participants for service, and that service cannot be effaced or minimized by the mere fact that they were not enrolled or that the regiment to which they belonged was not called out by a governor or by some military authority. Surely these should not be governing factors in a matter like this. I should like to know from the minister upon what principle he declines to recognize their claim.

The minister has not declined to recognize any claim; the minister has nothing to do with it. The law is here on the statue-book, clear and distinct: any officer, non-commissioned officer or man who comes within the law and the regulations under the law gets the bounty.
Then, what is the trouble?

The trouble is this:
Take, for instance, the Kingsville company, in Essex county. I have not the slightest doubt in my mind that the Kingsville company was organized, went to the front and was on duty for a couple of weeks. But this was not a company within the law, and accordingly the bounty claims committee, who are sworn officers of the best standing in the country, cannot see their way clear legally to recommend payment of the bounty to these men.
Why not change the law?

When this Bill was introduced two years ago, we told the minister that he would have a If t of trouble over the words ' called out.' T1 ,e minister will now realize that we were pointing out the true state of affairs. The difficulty has arisen, and I think the minister is getting into more trouble by trying to stick to the legal definition of what constituted being called out than he would have if he allowed common sense to prevail. I cannot see on what prinieple a man is to be paid for defending his country, but if you are going to recognize the principle of paying men for defending their country, surely those referred to by the hon. member for Haldimand ought to come under the principle or the principle should be made broad enough to include them. If the words ' called out ' are not broad enough, change the words. Then take the case of the four men in Charlotte county to which I have referred, who were sworn in and who were on the spot where there was an attempted invasion; surely these men should be included. Why does the minister not change the law and make it cover the men really entitled to it, and so change it that the 12,000 men in Nova Scotia who performed annual drill and who are not entitled to it shall not get the $100. Let us get down to

common, sense. This is the time and the place to change this law. I am sorry the minister is extending the time, he should be able to close it all up by the end of this year. I consider this one of the most unmanly, one of the most umCanadian pieces of legislation ever passed in this House. It is something that should never have been done. They should never be paid for doing what common decency and humanity demands of them, defend their homes and firesides. Where a man is incapacitated by reason of his service, or his earning power is decreased, then provision should be made for him. But for the man who simply does his duty there should be no reward of this kind. I fail to see how the minister is inculcating any spirit of loyalty or any other qualities that tend to make manly men of the people of Canada. But if he is going to do this, why cannot he do it in a simple straight-forward, business manner?

In 1870, after the Red
river rebellion, a grant of land wasi made to volunteers who took part in that rebellion. In 1885, at the conclusion of the Northwest rebellion, a grant of land wias made to certain volunteers. I am sorry to say that the Northwest Mounted Police did not get a grant. I have always felt that, even if they were on regular service, they should have received the grant the same as the others. After the South African war, the volunteers who went to the front were given grants of land. Thus there were three precedents established, and my good friend knows as well as I that these old veterans of '66 and '70 felt that a slight had been placed on them by their service not having been recognized. Rightly or wrongly we got mixed up in the matter.
Mixed up, that is right.

I am free to admit it is mixed up. My hon. friend told me at the start that I was laying up a peck of trouble for myself, and he told me truly; but I knew it at the time, and I accepted the trouble in order to satisfy the old fellows who, in all parts of Canada, turned out loyally and well in '66 and '70. I venture to say that, considering the number of claims presented, there are fewer dissatisfied than has. been the case with any similar number of applicants in any matter of this kind.
There cannot be very many dissatisfied in Nova Scotia.

I know that is a sore subject with my hon. friend. He has been trying to smooth his way down with his Nova Scotia friends. He put his foot in it the other night. I met Sir Charles Tupper when he was going to England last year. I asked him the details of this matter. He told me that the news was received in Halifax on the 17th of March, 1866, that a steamer had actually left Eastport, laden to the gunwales with ex-soldiers of the southern war, ready for a raid on any country; and that steamers were leaving Boston and New York to land on the shores of Nova Scotia. They were to enter the ports at night and to raid the banks, etc., and to make other depredations. Tne veteran statesman told me the story very lucidly. He said that from every headland the beacon fires were buming. Word was passed by telegraph as far as possible, and by men in the saddle and in boats, and in a day or two at the nearby points men rallied in a splendid way. I think I am justified in saying that upwards of 50,000 m^n turned out in March, not for annual drill, but for active service. Senator Power is always proud to refer to the days when there was universal compulsory service in Nova Scotia, and he still takes the ground that there should he compulsory service in all Canada. But, -compulsory service, or service without any compulsion other than the call to arms, the record shows how these old fellows, or young fellows, in overwhelming numbers turned out in every town in Nova Scotia, actually expecting an invasion of the country. Many of them were not armed, but came with pitchforks ready to defend their homes and firesides. Rightly or wrongly they are included in the Bill. As far as I am concerned, every man who answered that call, a legal call, is going to be recognized. The others who did not chance to be officially organized, cannot come under the Bill. There must be a line drawn somewhere. If we change that to make it more flexible, there will be kickers still; all the fellows who did work in '66 and '70 will demand the grant. I think that the simplest and best way is to give it to those who were called out for active service under the law, and if a poor fellow happened to be out and not under the law, that is his misfortune.
Can the minister inform me what number of applications have been received from Ontario and Quebec?
The figures were given the other day; I have not them with me at the moment.
Humour is now tnat about two men are being paid for every one called out.

I would be very sorry to believe such a rumour. My hon. friend is a distinguished representative of the province of Quebec, and I would be very sorry to insult the good people of Quebec by circulating any such slander on that province.
I did not hear it in Quebec; it came from Ontario. We have a precedent for that sort of thing in the payment of pensions in the United States.
The hon. memiber is the only one who has dared to assume responsibility for circulating such a rumour.

I asked for the figures first and the minister said he had not the figures.
Mr. MA0DQNA2LD: In regard to the position of the men of Nova cSotia who were applying for bounty under this Act, as the minister has said, the situation in Nova Scotia was a peculiar one in this regard, that compulsory militia service had existed there for a long period of years. Previous to Confederation every young man within the ages prescribed undeT the law was a member of the active militia. In my county alone ten regiments were drilled practically every year, and the interest manifested in the county was typical of the feeling throughout the whole province. I think that Nova Scotia was the only province in the Dominion in which compulsory services existed at that time. The Government's proclamation was issued in March, 1866, under circumstances which led the Governor and his advisors in the city of Halifax to believe that the province was in danger of an invasion. The situation in our province was peculiar at that time. For the preceding five years the people of Nova Scotia had been accustomed to seeing in every harbour and inlet round the coast privateers and vessels of war, connected both with the north and south, taking refuge in Nova Scotia ports during storms. The people were under the impression that at any moment some of those engaged in the Fenian cause might come to Nova Scotia. It cannot be urged for one moment that the Governor did not believe he had good and sound reasons for issuing the
fMr. C. Mareil.]
proclamation. He was a distinguished British soldier, and one of the last governors we had previous to Confederation. The men who turned out did not do so in response to the request to come to their annual drill, for that did not take place till later in the year. The commission that was appointed by the department to investigate the question called some of the most reputable people in the whole province as witnesses, men whose standing left no room for doubt as to the accuracy of their information, and the evidence was overwhelming to the effect that the special call immediately following the proclamation in the month of April was responded to, practically to a man, by every one who belonged to the active militia at that time.
A great many who were too old under the law turned out also.

I do not think my
hon. friend the Minister of Militia knew the facts as they existed in regard to Nova Scotia when he first came to Parliament with this proposition. When resolutions were previously moved in this House in regard to this matter I do not think hon. gentlemen were aware of the condition of affairs in Nova Scotia at that time, when members of the active militia were called out under all the official regulations that could obtain in any country. When this Bill first came before Parliament in 1912, the minister did not know and did not learn for a year afterwards that it applied eo generally .as it now does in our province. The provisions of the Act are eminently proper having regard to what has been done in similar cases, but the position of the hon. member for Carleton as to whether it is wise for countries to recognize services of this kind is a matter of argument. When the Act was drafted for dealing with this recognition of service at the time of the Fenian raid, it stipulated the safeguards that should exist: first, that the person called out should be a member of the active militia, for otherwise people would be coming forward with more or less degree of reason to assert that they volunteered here and there without any particular justification except their latent patriotism and in response to no recognized authority; and secondly, that the members of the active militia must have been called out by the regularly constituted authority in the province. Those are the two conditions which must exist before any one is entitled to the bounty. Those conditions existed in our province and it unexpectedly turns out on account of compulsory service

and the conditions to which I have referred, that in Nova Scotia a very much larger number of men than the minister and the House ever anticipated are entitled to be paid the bounty under the provisions of this law. I think it is only proper that this statement, which cannot he questioned, should be placed on ' Hansard ' so that every one will understand the circumstances in our province at that time.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. McCURDY (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
When this resolution was introduced on May 6, the hon. member for Carleton, in his usual vigorous style expressed himself even more forcibly than he has to-night, and made representations regarding the province of Nova Scotia which I think should not pass unchallenged. I intended at that time to controvert some of the statements which he made, but owing to the lateness of the hour-the House sat very late that night-and in deference to the request of the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition I deferred answering him till the second reading of the Bill. In the debate on the 6th of May the hon. member for Carleton addressing his remarks to the Minister of Militia said:
Does my hon. friend believe that there are 15,000 militia men in Nova Scotia to-day, 60 years of age, who were members of the militia at that time? It is not possible. I believe thousands of men in Nova Scotia have been paid who were barely born at the time of the Fenian raid, and my hon. friend knows it. He believes it anyway. It is simply a scandal.
. . . But the minister has sane business moments, and he knows that a great fraud is being perpetrated upon his department by the people of Nova Scotia.
.	.	. I repeat that the manner in which
these 15,000 people in Nova Scotia have been paid the bounty is simply a scandal.
Members of the House realize that owing to the prominence of the hon. member for Carleton in debates on all questions that come up for consideration in this House, his statement in this matter is bound to make a very serious and very unfortunate impression, particularly in view of the practical failure of his colleagues to repudiate the statements of the hon. member.
The hon. member for Pictou has outlined in a few words the conditions under which the militia of that day were ordered out for service. Anyone who talks sneeringly of the loyal and spontaneous response of the militia forces in Nova Scotia does a grave injustice to the militia of that province. Compulsory service was the law' in Nova Scotia nrior to Confederation. The population of the province in 1861 was
330,857; the active militia force of the province in 1866 at the time of the Fenian raid is reported at 58,031, or almost as large a number as the total .militia drilled last year in the whole of Canada.
It is true that no clash of arms occurred between the Fenian Raiders and His Majesty's loyal forces in Nova Scotia, but following the stirring martial events that occurred in the United States in the preceding five years a general feeling of uneasiness prevailed throughout the whole province. It was currently reported in Nova Scotia,, in March, 1866, that ships had been assembled by the Fenians in New England waters for descent on Nova Scotia, and on the 16th of March of that year direct statements to this effect were received by Sir Charles Tupper, at that time Dr. Tupper and Premier of the Province. On the following day the proclamation was issued calling out all members of the militia liable to perform military service in time of war. This proclamation was immediately and loyally responded to. The oath of allegiance was administered, and active drilling by practically all the battalions was carried on for from five to twenty days in different parts of the province.
It is estimated that between twenty-five per cent and thirty-five per cent of the 58,031 ordered out for active service at that time, are still alive.
I do not think it would be natural to expect that those who are turned out at that time, and who are still living, should not apply for this bounty. They are entitled to be rewarded for their services, they turned out in accordance with the proclamation and they fulfilled the conditions outlined in the Act. I do not think it lies in the mouth of the hon. member for Carleton to make the statement that he has made that a fraud has been perpetrated on the Minister of Militia and Defence by the-militiamen of Nova Scotia.
My hon. friend also states that the minister has not handled this matter in a businesslike way. As a matter of fact, the need for the present resolution comes because he approached the matter as a business man should. A large numbeT of applications were received, and the minister sent a commission to the province of Nova Scotia to ascertain at first hand, and as expeditiously as possible, the facts and the conditions under which the militia was mustered and this service performed. This commission was composed of two members of the Militia Council, Mr. Charles T. Panet and Mr. E. A. P. White, and to these were

added a local commissioner with local knowledge in each county. That commission was in a position to get the most accurate information possible. The procedure occupied some time, and before it was physically possible to complete the investigation and complete the payment of bounties, the time authorized in the Act of April, 1, 1912, had expired, and therefore this resolution is necessary to have the time extended.
The commission referred to sat in all of the counties of Nova Scotia. I had the pleasure of being present at all the sittings of the commission which were held in Shelburne and Queens. At these hearings a large number of veterans presented themselves and tendered their evidence. These included the leading and most reputable citizens in the county. As far as my knowledge goes, the statement of the hon. member for Carteton that some of these men were not born when these raids took place is absolutely and totally at variance with the facts. It is not difficult to estimate within a few years the age of any person. I am as morally certain as I can be of anything that none of these men, hundreds of whom I personally saw and talked to, fall within the limit mentioned by my hon. friend. When my hon. friend seeks to impugn the honesty of these veterans, I want to say frankly that I resent such an imputation. I cannot dissent too strongly from the opinion which he has expressed, and I wish to resent, on behalf of these rugged old veterans the slurs which he has sought to cast on their honesty.
There is another aspect of this question that is perhaps more controversial, and to which I think I should allude. I deplore the fact that politics have been drawn into the discussion of the question. My attention was called not long since to a circular letter which was sent out in large numbers by Liberal members in Nova Scotia, and which, among other things, contains the following:
The grant to Nova Scotia veterans was largely due to the energy displayed by some of our Nova Scotia Liberal members.
It is certainly news to the members of this House that the Nova Scotia Liberal members displayed any great amount of energy in forwarding the interests of the Fenian Raid veterans. The circulation of this statement makes it necessary, oir permissible at any rate, that I should contradict the assertion therein contained which assertion, I believe, is clearly at variance with the facts. Any one who will follow

the discussions in the House of the proposed grant to the Fenian Raid veterans can see that, net only have the Liberal members from Nova Scotia collectively and and as a body not assisted in securing this grant, but they have time and again, as the vote was called for, voted against such a recognition of their services.
If there is one characteristic that the *average Nova Scotia Liberal member of Parliament possesses more than another, that characteristic is ' party regularity.' He can always be depended upon to respond to the party whip. I do not seek to depreciate that characteristic in these representatives of the people, and I think that the different representatives themselves would be the last, to wish to proclaim themselves to their constituents as being other than stolid followers of the Liberal party, its politics, and principles. That being so, the case regarding the Fenian Raid veterans and the question as to the attitude of the Liberal members, can be definitely and finally settled by ascertaining what was the attitude officially of that party. In order to ascertain the official attitude of the party I would refer the committee to page 1089 of 'Hansard,' 1910-11. The responsible Minister of Militia in the late Administration was Sir Frederick Borden.

Doe3 my horn, friend mean to say that the present Minister of Militia knew, when, he came to Parliament with this resolution, that there were 15,000 men in Nova Scotia who were entitled to this grant?	.
I think the hon. gentleman's question might properly be directed to the Minister of Militia, who is in his seat.
Did the hon. member far North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), when he moved his resolution, know that there were only 15,000 men entitled to this grant?

That is a question also that should be directed to the hon. member for North Grey.
The responsible Minister of Militia in the late Administration was Sir Frederick Borden; he was the man who could authoritatively propound1 the Liberal dogma. He was .asked by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro):
Does this Government intend, during the present session, bringing down any legislation with reference to the grant of lands or money to the veterans of 1866 and 1870?

To which the reply was:
The Government has come to the conclusion that it is not in the public interest to grant public lands except as provided by law upon condition of residing and settlement. It is not intended to recommend a grant of money in view of the fact that pensions were granted at the time to wounded and to the families of those who were killed in the Fenian Raid engagements.
He said:
It is not in the public interest to grant public lands and it is not intended to recommend a grant of money.
There is nothing vague, obscure, or indefinite about that answer. It is positive, explicit, categorical. That was the official pronouncement of the Liberal party towards the .suggested Fenian Raid grant, the attitude of members opposite one and all present in the House when the question was voted on.
I would draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that he is making a statement that is rather wide with reference to hon. gentlemen opposite.
In what regard?
When he says that the resolution introduced in 1910 was opposed by all hon. members opposite. Does the hon. member intend to convey that idea?

I will repeat my statement if it is not clear to my hon, friend. What I said was that all Liberal members present in the House, when votes were at various times taken on this question, voted to sustain the policy of the Liberal Government as propounded by Sir Frederick Borden.
Is my hon. friend aware of the fact that the motion was made as a motion of want of confidence in the late Government?

I am not at present
referring to a motion; I am referring to a question put upon the Order Paper and answered by the then Minister of Militia, Sir Frederick Borden, who was best qualified to propound the Liberal dogma.

I understood that my
hon. friend was referring to the motion of the hon. member for North Grey, and I wish to point out that that motion was moved as a want of confidence motion, on Mr. Fielding moving the House into Committee of Supply. If the hon. member for North Grey was anxious about the matter he took
the wrong course by moving it as a want of confidence motion.

My hon. friend
apparently has not heard me aright. I was referring to the answer of Sir Frederick Borden, then Minister of Militia, who stated that it wras not intended to recommend a grant of money. Possibly my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) may contend that Sir Frederick Borden wias not qualified to speak for the Administration of that day, but I think we may fairly assume that his statement was a clear representation of the policy of the Government of which he was a member. All the Liberal members who were present in the House when motions came up at various times, to provide recognition for the veterans, voted against the payment of any Fenian Raid bounties. That is how those who profess themselves so solicitous now in the interests of the Fenian Raid veterans acted when their friends occupied the treasury benches, and at which time alone their activity and interest could have been of service to the veterans.
But fortunately for the claimants for the bounty a change of Administration took place in 1911 and one of the first acts of the new Administration was the introduction of a Bill by the Hon. Sam. Hughes, Minister of Militia, providing for a grant of one hundred dollars to each veteran ' called out for active service in the year 1866' or 'whom the Government of Canada called out for active service after Confederation in the year 1870, except in the two battalions of riflemen formed for service in the Northwest.' Liberals in power were opposed to and repeatedly voted against the granting of aid to Fenian raid veterans, but now when a Conservative Government assumes the responsibility of making this long-delayed grant, Liberal members actually send circulars throughout the country containing this statement:
The grant to Nova Scotia veterans was largely due to the energy displayed by some of our Nova Scotia Liberal members.
I frankly confess that had I not seen with my own eyes an original letter containing this statement, I would not have believed that any hon. member opposite
had signed such a letter.
What does the hon. gentleman mean by that ?

I shall have great
pleasure in sending to my hon. friend the original of one of these letters.

I do not care whether I see one or not; it would not interest me a bit. I want to correct any impression the hon. gentleman may seek to give the House that I ever issued a letter in my life about the Fenian raid bounty, and I never saw one written by anybody else. Of course, that is not saying that such a letter was sent out.

The letter I have in my possession is signed by Mr. Bowman B.
Law, member for Yarmouth, and a copy can 'be seen by reference to page 3508 of * Hansard ' of May 6, 1914.
Mr. Law supported the measure just as much as you did.

I understand that other
Liberal members sent out similar letters to their constituents': In fact, there seems to be a wonderful similarity in the different letters sent out by the members of the Opposition; their minds seem to have been running in the same channel on the subject.
In reply to the question put just now by the hon. member for Pictou, I beg to say that Liberal members supported their administration when in power and declined' to have these grants voted to the Fenian raid veterans, but they did not have the courage of their convictions to oppose it when the positions were reversed and when the Conservative Government proposed the grant,

Would my hon.
friend allow me; perhaps I can help him out. Would he be good enough to tell the House when he discovered that the Bill of 1912 permitted Nova Scotians to the number of 15,000 to apply for this money?

It is very kind of my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) to endeavour to help me out, and I appreciate it very much. Of course, we all understand that the hon. gentleman's interruptions are always attempted with the idea of assisting an opponent. I repeat that hon. gentlemen opposite, when their friends were in power and when they were therefore in a position to make effective legislation, voted solidly against recognition of these claims, but when, fortunately, the positions were reversed, and they found their votes would no longer prevent the passing of the legislation introduced by this Government, and when they knew that any credit accruing from the payment of these claims would come to the government of the day, they had not the courage of their convictions, and, instead of still opposing the Bill, they allowed it to go without op-

position. In view of the history of this question, as shown by the records of this House, nobody in the country will have any doubt as to whom the credit is due for this grant to the veterans.

! want to refer for a moment to the statement of my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), and to endorse what the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) has said in resenting any imputation against the good faith and patriotism of the veterans of Nova Scotia. I was surprised that my hon. friend from Carleton again referred to this matter to-night, after the information we gave him on the occasion of the previous
10 p.m. discussion. It is perfectly clear to any man who will honestly look into the facts, that the number of Nova Scotia veterans who are applying for the bounty at the present time is not excessive, considering the population of the province in 1866. It is well known, and it will be found in the reports to the government of the day, that over fifty thousand men turned out to repel the threatened invasion, and a great many of them were doubtless young men. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) should remember that the minimum age. fixed was sixteen years, and everybody knows how anxious every boy in the province would be to take his part on an occasion of that kind. It is not at all correct to say that there are not to-day fifteen thousand, or twenty thousand, or at most twenty-five thousand men in the province of Nova Scotia who are sixty-four years of age. If my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) would take the trouble to look up the census returns, he will find verification of my statement. The whole male population of the province between sixteen years and sixty were ordered out to drill, and I understand they turned out. It is quite true they never did any active service in the sense that I understand active service, but they made preparation for it, and as a matter of law they come under the Act we are now considering.
I hope my hon. friend from Carleton will not repeat the statement any further, because there is ample proof in the records of the province of Nova Scotia to show that that statement is not correct. But, referring for a moment to what my hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) has been discussing, I want to point out to him that as I understand the situation, the Government did not intend when they introduced this measure in 1912, to give anything to

the veterans of Nova Scotia. I think I can show this from the records of the short discussion that took place in the House when the Act was passed. I suppose the hon. gentleman was in the House, and if he was, he would be expected to raise his voice in favour of the veterans of Nova Beotia which I understand he did not do.
I was not in the House.

At all events, there is ample proof that the Government never intended to give anything to Nova Scotia veterans. This proof was submitted to the House by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) a few evenings ago, that the 'Government did not know they were giving one dollar to the veterans of Nova Scotia when they introduced the Bill in 1912. If the hon. gentleman will refer to page 6256 of ' Hansard ' of 1912, he will find that when the Bill was introduced, I asked the minister the following question:
Will the Act apply to men who were called out to drill? I understand that in the province of Nova Scotia a number of men were drafted and collected at some particular place, ana submitted themselves to some few weeks drill preparatory to going to the front, but they never did go. What will be done in the case of those men?
And here we have the answer:
Mr. Hughes (Victoria) : The law says they must have been called out for active service and the man who is called out for drill is not called out for active service. He has been called out in anticipation of meeting the enemy.
These men were called out for active service and not for drill. The Bill is clear and these men are clearly entitled to the bounty. The geographical location of the volunteer does not matter.

My hon. friend is quite mistaken. I continued the inquiry:
I have no doubt it was in anticipation of service but the raid, as everybody remembers, was short. These men were not required to go to the front, but they were drafted. They went through the process of being drafted, selections were made from each regiment, and those men selected were taken from different places and submitted to drill preparatory to going to the front, but there was no call for them to go to the front.
Mr. Hughes: My hon. friend will realize from his legal knowledge that if the official notification to the officers in the locality called out these troops in a certain year for preparatory drill only, then they do not come under the Act. If they were called out for active service-as certain of the Nova Scotia volunteers were called out, and went to the front-they do come under the Act.
That is the statement-they were to be called out for active service, but it was for those who went to the front that this bounty was provided. There is some further discussion, but this is the material point raised at that time by myself. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) says he was not present, but other Conservative members from Nova Scotia were present, and so far as I recollect not one of them raised his voice in favour of the veterans of Nova Scotia. It is clear that when the Bill was introduced in 1912 the Government had no intention of giving one dollar to the veterans of Nova Scotia.'

Then, will the hon. gentleman be good enough to say why we included the word ' Nova Scotia' in the list?
Mr. SINCLAIR; Because, as I undeiv stood the hon. gentleman to say, there were a few Nova Scotia veterans who had gone to the front to assist New Brunswick, and these were in active service. That was drawn to his attention. To show that the Government had no intention of giving this bounty to the veterans of Nova Scotia, when Parliament met in the following year, there was another discussion which I will quote. This was on the 26th of March, 1913, and is reported at page 6418 of * Hansard ' of that year. I again directed the attention of the Prime Minister to this matter. Here is an extract from ' Hansard ' of that date:
I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Hughes), and, in his absence, that of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), to the question of the bounties to Fenian raid veterans. The rumour is abroad in Nova Scotia that all parties who were ordered out to drill at the time of the Fenian agitation was on in 1866, are to be included in the bounty that is to be given to Fenian raid veterans. We were told last year that only such veterans as had seen active service were to receive that bounty. I understand that the Governor of Nova Scotia issued a proclamation in 1866 authorizing preparations for meeting the Fenian raids that were expected at that date. Very many people turned out, underwent drill for several weeks, and subsequently, when the draft was made, certain people were selected out of the number that had been engaged in the drill to go to the front if they were required. As the Prime Minister knows no steps of that kind were necessary, and with few exceptions no person from that province went to the front. Are the parties who subjected themselves to drill and who made preparations to go to the front if they were required entitled to share in the bounty that is to be given to Fenian raid veterans?
Whose question is that?

I never claimed credit. I said it was a matter in which party politics should not be mixed up. But what I objected to was that hon. gentlemen opposite should have statements published like this:
The grant to Nova Scotia was largely due to the energy displayed by some of our Nova Scotia Liberal members.

That statement is quite correct. But my hon. friend will not say that his colleagues in the province of Nova Scotia did not endeavour to make capital out of this discussion. It has been brought up on the occasion of every municipal election that has taken place in the province, at least in that part of it with which I am well acquainted. The votes of the people have been asked for because of the $100 which is to be paid to the veterans by this benevolent Government. Everyone in North Cape Breton knows that this matter figured largely in the recent election in Victoria county. I have before me a letter written by the gentleman who afterwards became local member for the county of Victoria, which practically tells the people of that county that even

if they do make false statements in their applications for the bounty, no harm will come to them because he will stand behind them; that he has sufficient influence with the Government to see that a man who makes a false statement in applying for the bounty will not be punished and that perjury will be condoned. That is the attitude taken by our friends in the province of Nova Scotia, who have endeavoured ever since this Act was passed to make political capital out of it.
Will my hon. friend read Mr. McLeod's letter wherein he condones perjury ?

The letter is dated Bad-deck, February 6. 1914, and is as follows:
To our Fenian Raid Veterans.
Deaf Sir,-X wish to congratulate those of you who have received your bounty. To those who have not I wish to say that I am informed from Ottawa that although your application for the Fenian Raid bounty has been passed, there may be a little further delay before you get your check. The cause of this delay is that a further vote of Parliament is needed to complete the payment of deferred and belated applications. You are therefore absolutely sure ot getting your check very soon.
There is a report that many of the' applicants were not really sure that they had drilled in March and April, 1866, and consequently had no right to swear to it. I think I can assure you that nothing will be done to our friends in that connection.
That is pretty plain. Mr. McLeod, the candidate of the Conservative party has heard that certain men had no right to swear that they served at the date required by law in 1866, but he says:
I think I can assure you that nothing will be done in that connection.
In other words, perjure yourselves if necessary, and I will see that nothing will be done to you. The letter goes on to say:
Many false and misleading claims are being made by our opponents concerning the granting of the Fenian Raid bounty. However, one fact must forever stand out in the history of this county, and that is! that it was the Borden Government that passed the law giving the bounty to the veterans of the Fenian Raid of 1866. They are all old men to-day, and the present generation is proud of them for the noble manner in which they sprung to arms in defence of our country in those stern times when the rivals of Britain had covetous eyes on this Canada of ours.
After nearly fifty years you are called upon again to take a stand in the defence of your country and help to lift it out of the rut of slipshod government. I therefore ask you to vote for me on February the 12th and for an era of greater expansion for the splendid province of Nova Scotia.
Faithfully yours,
(Sgd) Philip McLeod.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he will lay that document on the table of the House? I would like to have a look at it.
I have no objection.
What good will that do?

It does not make
any difference what good it will do; it is my privilege to ask that it be laid on the table of the House.

The hon. gentleman
must understand that this is not the original letter, but it has been given to me as a true and correct copy of the original letter He will find it in ' Hansard ' to-morrow.
I want to say now that that is not the original letter written by Mr. McLeod and addressed to the electors of Victoria county.
Will you produce the original letter?
I cannot produce it here and now, but that is not the original letter.
I am in a position to say that that is a copy of the original letter, and I defy my hon. friend, the hon. member for Kings, N.S., to produce an original that differs from that letter.
This is a very serious matter. Any lawyer does not need to be a judge to know that if you have the original you have to produce it. Let us have the original.

The copy is just as good as the original in this case. The hon. gentleman will find this letter in almost any house in the county of Victoria if he will look for it, because they were scattered broadcast all over the country. Every veteran, I presume, received one. It is clear to me, and, I think, clear to everybody else, that the Government did not intend to give this bounty to the veterans of Nova Scotia at the time the Act was passed, but that it was afterwards decided that they were entitled to it by reason of the interpretation of the law and the discovery of the proclamation ordering the men out for active service on that occasion. If we got the bounty by a legal construction placed on the Act which the Government never intended, we owe them no thanks for it.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to the question of the widows of veterans who died prior to the 1st day of April, 1912.
I have a number of applications in my desk from widows who claim to be entitled to the bounty and whose husbands died prior to that date. In one case the veteran died on March 27, 1912, only three or four days before the date fixed by the minister, and there are other cases of a like nature. I submit that there is no principle upon which the minister can deny the bounty to the widows of veterans who died prior to that date. I have heard him give no satisfactory explanation on that point; but, from the answer which he was kind enough to give to >a question I asked him in the early days of the session, I assumed that when the Bill would be introduced these widows would be provided for. The minister on that occasion said very frankly that provision would be made in the law to pay everybody who is entitled to the bounty. I submit 'that the widows of veterans who died prior to the first day of April, 1912, are just as much entitled to the bounty as the widows of veterans who died after that date. I had hoped that the minister, in taking a step forward with the Bill to-night, would have made some provision in that regard. If he does not intend to make an effort to do so, I myself would like to move an amendment to the Bill. I wish to know whether or not the minister has really decided that he will not take any action with regard to that phase of the matter.

The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens protests against the introduction of politics into the question of the Fenian Raid Bounty Act. I suppose that so long as politics is politics, so long will it creep into the administration of a great many of the public services of this country, whether one would desire it or not. I think it is hardly fair for my 'hon. friend to complain that some hon. .gentlemen on this side have written letters .perhaps with too much enthusiasm assigning credit to the Liberal party for the passage of the Fenian Raid Act. He should be generous enough to remember that hon. gentlemen supporting the Government from Nova Scotia have more than once claimed [DOT]the entire credit for the Government which they support for the passage of this Bill. That is a very unjustifiable claim on their *part and so long as that is made by hon. gentlemen, opposite they must expect occasionally to hear some similiar claims from this side of the House. At no time in the history of this Parliament did this question come before it in quite the same manner in which it is found set forth in the

present Aet. As the hon. member for Guygborough has pointed out, when this Bill was passed it was not known by the Minister of Militia or by the Government or by any hon. gentleman in this House that it would be or could be construed as liberally as it afterwards was. Hon. gentlemen will concede that I am correct in that proposition.
No.

The hon. member for
Kings dissents, but I challenge him to establish his denial of the proposition which I have just set forth.

I do not have to
establish it.

The hon. gentleman has to establish it, because the Minister of Militia has before this admitted the correctness of the position I now take, and it has been abundantly proved that at the time this Act was submitted to Parliament it was not expected or intended that it would be construed so liberally as it has since been.
It is not a question of construing the Act but merely of producing the evidence.
That js perfectly correct in administering the Act; but what I mean to say is that the Act as construed to-day is much wider than was the intention of the Government when introducing it.
Absolutely identical.
I think the hon. gentleman is incorrect in his assertion. I think he has admitted the correctness of my statement on previous occasions.
Produce the evidence.

I have not the evidence before me. I did not, however, rise to discuss that phase of the question. I never issued a letter to my constituents in regard to this matter, and do not propose to do so. I agree with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) that it is very regrettable indeed that there has been injected into the administration of this matter so much party politics.
Mr. MeCURDY: I did not say that; I did not say that politics had been injected into the administration.

If you did not make
that statement perhaps you would like now to make it and thus agree with me? The hon. gentleman is quite correct, he did not

say that and I did not intend to convey the impression that he did. I hope, however that he agrees with me. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens objects unfairly, I think, to gentlemen on this side saying that they did not oppose the principle of this Bill. This is true. I do say, however, that I object to the manner in which this Act has been administered. It has occupied altogether too much time. The letter read by the hon. member for Guysborough clearly indicates one of the necessary and natural results of a loose administration of the Act and of the unnecessarily lengthy period taken for the completion of the work. That	letter would appear	to contain a promise on behalf of one man to secure for his political friends condonation of perjury, and I think that should be a very impressive warning to the minister to hasten the payments which are due or payable under this Act. I trust that he will not ask Parliament to give him until July 31, 1915, to complete payments. He should do it very much earlier.
During this session I asked the minister if in any respect he had furnished information to the Conservative Association of Halifax county, which in turn was forwarded to applicants. I received a very haughty negative from the minister to the effect that no official of the Halifax County Conservative Association ever received advice from his department respecting the administration of the Act or giving any departmental information in reference to applications.
Hear, hear.

I wish to read a letter issued by the Halifax County Conservative Association ajnd signed toy the secretary, which had wide circulation not only in the county of Halifax, but in pretty nearly every county in Nova Scotia. This letter,, which I am about to read, was received by an applicant for Fenian Raid bounty, and it is only one of a great number which I have in my possession. It is written on the official paper of the Halifax County Conservative Association. The telephone number and post office box and building of the association rooms are given. The let-/ ter is as follows:
The Halifax County Liberal-Conservative Association.
Halifax, N.S., October 13, 1913.
Dear Sir,-I am advised by the Militia Department that your application for the Fenian Raid bounty is being held for the following reasons:	' Tear of service not stated '. You

had better re-apply for the bounty and correct this error, and if you call at my office at any time X will be glad to render you any assistance in this matter.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) W. G. Poster,
Secretary.
Hundreds of letters similar to that have been circulated throughout the whole province. I submit to the minister that it is a moat unfair letter to circulate. It is a-direct intimation to applicants for the Fenian Raid bounty that if they called at the rooms of the Halifax County Conservative Association their applications would,' possibly receive better and speedier treatment than if they went elsewhere. HoVr many applicants receiving letters of that kind from the secretary of the Conservative Association of the county of Halifax would not think that it perhaps had some special significance? The minister will appreciate my point and further the fact that the letter conveyed to the recipient the idea that the Minister of Militia was in direct correspondence with the secretary of a political association. I want the minister to look into this matter immediately, and see that it does not occur again.

I have nothing to do with circulars issued by some Conservative or some Grit associations in Nova Scotia. If they issue a dozen circulars I shall not tag up and down Nova Scotia following up various associations. Let the hon. member produce a line from the department of that kind and I will be prepared to investigate it.

My hon. friend must
pay more respect to a letter of this kind than he would to a letter like the one read" by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens.
Not a particle.
