That is not one calling for official recognition; but here is one in which the secretary of the Halifax Conservative Association states that he is advised by the Militia Department of the causes for the delay in the granting of bounty to an applicant. This is a condition of affairs which I may fairly ask the Minister of Militia to take cognizance of. I know that the secretary of this association (Mr. Foster) must have had information from the department.

I know that Mr. Foster had no information from the department,
either directly or indirectly. It was a mere guess game the same as the Liberals played.

I do not see how the
information could have been obtained otherwise.

What information is
conveyed?

The information is to
the effect that he was advised by the Militia Department that the application for the bounty made by the recipient of this letter was delayed by reason of the fact that the year of service was not stated in his application.
What is the date of the letter ?
October 13, 1913, and I want to assure the minister that this was not the only letter that was sent out.
That is, after the commission was around. All their proceedings were in open court.

There may be some explanation as to how this writer received his information. If there is I shall be very glad to receive it, but if special information has been furnished the secretary of the Conservative Association for the county of Halifax in respect to the administration of this Act I protest; I submit that it is unfair and I expect the Minister of Militia to prevent anything of that sort. If I am not correctly stating the facts I have no complaint whatever against the department, but I submit that payments due under this Act should be paid as quickly as possible. I think, and have always thought, that the minister should have despatched a number of officials from the service, particularly to the province of Nova Scotia where there are so many applicants, and they could have moved from county to county receiving applications and in certain cases practically paying the bounty on the spot. It has taken altogether too long to make the payments.

I might point out that
the Militia Department merely issues the warrants; the payment is made by the Finance Department. So far as the circular is concerned to which my hon. friend has referred, let me say at the outset that I was appealed to by members of the House for information-I am not breaking any confidences; I refuse to recognize any confidences in regard to public matters of this kind from any member, Liberal or Conservative. I challenge any member of

the House, Liberal or Conservative, from the Prime Minister downwards, to say that he ever got a list from me in regard to the province of Nova Scotia. When the list was prepared I sent a copy to the Prime Minister's office, and that is what was laid on the table of the House. The cords binding it were not cut, nor were the seals broken. The information that my hon. friend thinks was given by the department might have been obtained at the court, for the commission sat in open court. I had nothing to do with it, and never heard of it. I have the word of Mr. Charles Panet, who is the head of the organization, that no report was given to any member, either Liberal or Conservative. It was reported to me that a Liberal member of Parliament had been in his room several times, but there was nothing wrong about that. I spoke to Mr. Pane't about it. I said1: 'I am asked by a number of Liberal and also Conservatives to give certain facts. I have pointed out that it cannot be done under the regulations, and they have at once repudiated any further desire to get the information.' He said, and I have the utmost confidence in him, I believe what he says- that these gentleman had never once asked him for information, either directly or indirectly. So I may say, to the honour of hon. members on both sides of the House, that there has been no attempt to get information in an underhand way so far as I am aware. The little attempts to make political capital I simply laughed at. The only time I interfered was when I heard that some parties were seeking to get commissions on the bounties paid to certain veterans. I then caused one of the officers of the department to issue a notice that no commission was chargeable at all, and we took steps to ensure that the warrants should be issued direct to the applicants, so that no commission could be collected by any outside party.
I am quite satisfied with the minister's explanation. I just wanted an understanding. The writer of this letter was in error, I suppose, in saying he was advised by the Militia Department.
He might have thought the commission represented the Militia Department. I do not know what information the commission gave at the courts, as I was not present.
He did not get the facts from the Militia Department?

Nothing from me, and
Mr. Panet assures me he never gave any information directly or indirectly to anybody, and I have absolute faith in him. In regard to the point of the hon. member for Guysboro (Mr. Sinclair) I did not point out what veterans were entitled to the bounty, I did not bother looking up the Nova Scotia law or the proclamation; I do not know anything about it. The law on the statute-book states that every man who was called out for active service under the law is entitled to the bounty. That is the answer, and that is the answer I have always given to the beautifully-worded questions of my hon. friend. I simply stand by the law.

This question has been
discussed at more or less length, but I do not know that any useful purpose is being served. In a nutshell the position is this: Hon. gentlemen opposite were in power for fifteen years but never enacted any legislation of this kind. When the question was put to the Minister of Militia in the late Government, he stated that the Government did not intend to do this sort of thing. Shortly after the present Administration came into power, this Act was placed upon the statute-books and the credit is due to the Borden Administration. There is no question about it. If hon. gentlemen opposite propose to take credit for Government legislation they might as well cease their opposition to the Canadian Northern railway proposals and everything else. Apparently they are assuming equal responsibility for all Government legislation. My particular purpose in rising is to dissent entirely from the interpretation placed upon the letter of Philip McLeod by the hon. junior member for Halifax and the hon. member for Guysboro. Philip McLeod was the a local candidate in the county of Victoria. I had never seen or heard of that letter before to-night, but I do not believe it is susceptible of the interpretation that has been placed upon it by hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not for one moment assent to the proposal that it was Philip McLeod's intention to intimate to these veterans that they could perjure themselves with impunity because they were his friends. That was not his intention at all. I personally know of many old veterans who undoubtedly were out drilling and who could qualify for this bounty. Many of them are old men and very particular. They could not swear to the exact date. They say: I cannot swear that I drilled in the year 1866; I know I

was out drilling about that time and that my friends were out with me, and that I was served with a rifle; I have no reasonable doubt in my mind that I was out in 1866 but I do not want to swear to it. That is the position of many old men. After having conversed with them and inquired into the facts I have told them that they would be perfectly justified in making an affidavit that they were entitled to the bounty, and it is cases of this kind that Mr. McLeod had in mind. I must resent the imputation that Philip McLeod intended to lend himself to condone perjury.
I know Mr. McLeod personally; he is not a lawyer. He may perhaps have written that letter in a way which would bear such an interpretation as has been placed upon it, but even then I doubt that such an interpretation can be placed upon it. Knowing Mr. McLeod as I do, I have no doubt that such a thought was farthest from his mind, and that his idea in writing that letter was as I have suggested.

When the resolution
which is the basis of this Bill was under discussion some time ago, early in May, I, like my hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy), had not the opportunity of saying the few words I intended to say upon that occasion. 1 agree with the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) in the statement that there are many men to-day in Nova Scotia who are entitled to this bounty, but who are, nevertheless, too conscientious, too scrupulous, to make the declaration necessary under this law. I know two officers in the county of Cape Breton who refused absolutely to make the declaration because they had some conscientious scruples as to whether it was in March that they were called out. I know a gentleman who went to these officers and explained to them certain incidents that occurred in the course of the drill which took place on that occasion, but, by reason of the fact that they could not themselves remember the incidents, they refused to make application.
In view of the fact that there have been statements made in the House which would lead one to believe that there were some people in Nova Scotia who would commit perjury, I desire to make a remark or two upon that matter. I dare say there are some people in Nova Scotia who would commit perjury; I dare say there aTe people in the other provinces of Canada who would commit perjury, but I do not
think it is a fair assertion to say that any applicant for this bounty has committed perjury. If the statement was made by the Government, backed up by some very strong evidence, that any applicant had committed perjury, I would be the first to assist in the effort to obtain a conviction of that man. I am not going to place myself on record as saying that there are none who have made application but those who turned out and performed actual service at the time, but I do pot say that even these people committed wilful perjury. There may have been some confusion as between the special drill which took place in March, 1866, and the annual drill that occurred between June and September. It, is not at all surprising that 15,000 out of 57,000 in the province of Nova Scotia should be living at the present time, in view of the fact that the age at which these people did not voluntarily but were obliged to turn out and drill was between 16 and 60. I saw a list the other day from the district of Cheticamp, in the county of Inverness, and, according to that list, there were at that time only four men who came out who were over 45 years of age. As a matter of fact, the great majority of them, with the exception of 50 or 60, ranged from 16 to 24 years of age; so that it would not be surprising if every man who came out in that district should be living at the present time.
In reference to making political capital out of this matter, I admit that I did publish a circular letter in two of the papers in the county of Cape Breton telling persons who would be applicants for the Fenian Raid bounty that if there was anything I could do to assist them in making their applications I would be glad to do it.
I looked upon this as a duty incumbent upon me as the representative of the people in Parliament. I got the list submitted by the Minister of Militia, I wrote to each individual and explained the position of his application. That communication was accompanied by a letter to the effect that if there were any persons who had made application and whose names did not appear on the list, I would try and trace them up in the Militia Department. I found between eight and twelve people whose applications were made out, but which applications were, unfortunately, lost afterwards in the mail or through the negligence of the persons who made the applications. These matters were rectified as a result of whatever little vigilance I

gave to the question, and if I get any political revenue, so to speak, from it, I am very glad indeed to have it.
I do not adhere to the proposition that a person who comes out for his country is not entitled to pay. It is not a sound proposition, because when soldiers come out to fight for their country they are paid. If these gentlemen who make application for bounty had been present at the	annual camp	in	Nova
Scotia in 1866, or in any other province, they would have received their drill pay. These people came out in what at that time was the dead of winter, because I know men in Cape Breton who walked from twenty-five to forty miles on snow-shoes calling the men out to drill.
I do not think any of these men got paid in 1866. I think they gave their services absolutely free.
Suppose they did; I am saying that there is not a man who turns out to drill from one end of Canada to the other but receives some recompense.
I was merely strengthening my hon. friend's argument.

I do not think it is unfair that these men should receive some slight recompense; I think it is absolutely fair. As for what the Liberal party did in the fifteen years they were in power, I can only say to the hon. member for Cumberland that his party were in power for eighteen years previous to that and they did not seem to do very much.
Quite so, but they never refused to grant this bounty.
I think it will be shown before this discussion is over that they did.
If they did they are rectifying it now.

I am giving them all credit. As far as anything that was done in this House by either party is concerned, I do not think that we did anything to be ashamed of. The Bill received every assistance from this side of the House. I do not know of any one except my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), who advised the minister that he was going to get entangled in a great net as a result of bringing in this Bill.
And I told him the truth.

You certainly did; I admit that. But if hon. gentlemen opposite

say that the Liberal party has always opposed this proposition they are not telling the whole truth. I am not speaking for any of the members who were in this House in 1910 and 1911 and who. are hero now; they can speak for themselves. It is rather unfair for hon. gentlemen to say that the Liberal party were always lined up against this proposition. I did not line up against it but when the resolution was .introduced it had my hearty .support and I was in the House from the time that this Bill was in-trduced until it went through. I do not say that I assisted the Minister of Militia because he does not need my assistance in matters military but at the same time I was quite willing if, he needed any assistance, to do everything possible to further the Bill. I agree with my. hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that the Government in this country being regulated by party politics, they are bound to creep into everything. I am a commissioner and a notary public in my county but the only application I took was that of a friend of my own with whom I was visiting. He asked me to make out his application and I advised him that he .should get somebody else to do it, but in the end I took it. Applications were made by friends of mine and political capital was attempted to be made by the other side saying that these applications were no good. I do not begrudge the political capital which any party can make out of a piece of legislation. If I do a good thing I expect to make friends by it for the Liberal party in my part of the country, and if I' do anything that does not meet with the approbation of the people, I believe I would lose the support of several Liberals in my constituency. It is just as well for us to accept the broad facts.
I wish to point out to the Minister of Militia that it does not appear fair to say that because a man was living on the 1st of April, 1912, and died on the 2nd of April, 1912, that his widow or legal representative should receive one hundred dollars, whereas if he happened to die on the last day of March, 1912, his widow would receive nothing. I do not think that such a proposition commends itself even to the minister himself. It is true the line of demarcation must be drawn, but so long as it is provided that the widows-and I agree with that proposition-should receive this money, then the least the Act should provide is that the widow of any person,

whether he died on the 1st of June, 1866, or the 30th of April, 1912, should receive this bounty.

Would there not he
trouble in proving the facts about a man who died in 1866?
There would be no trouble; he would have to get the declaration of a comrade.
But he is dead.
His widow would know whether he went out or not, and at all events some comrade of his would be alive.
The Act only recognizes the volunteers who were alive on that date.

You recognize the
widows.

A man living on the

But you are certainly
recognizing widows.

Mr. 'CARROLL: You recognize first the widows, and then you recognize the estate if the widow is dead.
We recognize the widows of those who died since 1st April, 1912.

Suppose any of these
veterans who came out in 1866 under the proclamation in Nova Scotia, lost their lives directly or indirectly because of obeying that proclamation, would it not be absolutely fair that their now surviving widows would receive this bounty? With reference to the letters that were written by members from the province of Nova Scotia I have nothing to say. My hon. friend from Cumberland has said that it was not Mr. McLeod's intention that his letter should be construed as it has been. Perhaps it was not Mr. McLeod's intention that that letter should get into the hands of any other person 275
than the gentleman to whom it was sent, but I have no doubt that Mr. McLeod expected, and possibly received support from persons to whom he sent this letter. Whether they come from political friends or political opponents of mine, I say it is regrettable that such [letters should be circulated. It is also regrettable that people should be misled in connection with this matter. I might bring to the attention of the Minister of Militia one circumstance that came under my notice and I am	not	blaming	the Government	orthe minister in connection with it. In Glace Bay, a friend of mine, a Mr. Tobin, went	around with	the commission,	andan election was pending,	and11 p.m. letters were sent out broadcast through	the rural districts	of
that constituency to the effect that no person would obtain the bounty unless the application was endorsed by Mr. Tobin. Of course no such endorsement was necessary because I know that men got the bounty whose applications Mt. Tobin never saw; but this shows the way the thing has been worked politically. I do not mind a person obtaining political kudos so long as there is no misrepresentation, but I do object to men on either side of politics misrepresenting anything in connection with this question. I make these remarks, first to put myself square with what little connection I had with this Act and, in the second place, to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that section 4 should be so amended so as to include the widows of those who died previous to the coming into force of this Act on the 1st of April, 1912.

I wish to remind the minister that, when this question was under discussion in the House on a previous occasion, he stated that the resolution passed by the Legislature of Prince Edward Island was passed after the trouble was over. No doubt the minister was under that impression, but he is mistaken. The resolution is dated only one month after the proclamation was issued 'by the Governor of Nova Scotia. The proclamation in Nova Scotia was issued on the 17th March, 1866, and the resolution passed by the Legislature of Prince Edward Island is dated the 14th of April, 1866. I take it that the resolution passed by the Legislature of Prince Edward Island is equivalent or more than equivalen+ to the proclamation of the Governor of Nova Scotia. The words of that resolution are very strong:



Resolved, that in consequence of the threatened invasion of the British colonies by bands of Fenian marauders, this House pledges itself to place the whole of the revenue of the Island at the disposal of the Government for the purpose of organization of the militia and volunteers and for such other military purposes as may be deemed expedient for the protection and defence of the colonies.
Here were the whole resources of the provinces pledged for this purpose, a month after the militia of Nova Scotia was called out. There is evidence on record in Prince Edward Island that the Prince Edward Island militia were called out to drill just the same as the militia of Nova Scotia were called out to drill under the proclamation of the 17th of March, in preparation to repel the invasion.
They were called out in the middle of the winter; they were out in the month of January before the Legislature met. They were preparing as much as the militia of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to repel this raid. They are in exactly the same position as those of any other province, except that there was not a proclamation by the Governor. But the legislature spoke for the whole people, and all their resources were pledged to repel the invasion. Is not that as strong as a proclamation by the Governor of Nova Scotia or of any other province? I would suggest to the minister-I suggest it, I do not move it,-that the Bill should be amended by adding the words ' P. E. I. ' after ' N. B. ' in the fourth line of paragraph 2, and after the word ' service ' the words ' or in the case of Prince Edward Island drilled in pursuance of the resolution of the legislature of that province passed on the 14th of April, 1866.' Perhaps the Minister can suggest something better, 'but I think the province should receive some recognition. That is my contention; and I am not going to detain the House or attempt to make this a political question. I have been rather amused at the hon. members from Nova Scotia who said they were not going to make political capital out of this though there is no -doubt they are attempting to do so. I wish simply to have the Act amended so that the volunteers who were called out in Prince Edward Island in 1866 should be placed on the same footing asi volunteers called out in the other provinces. And I would especially direct the attention of the Government to this resolution passed on the 14th of April, 1866, which is of record in -the Journals of the Prince Edward Island Legislature and which, I think, is stronger in effect than the proclamation of the Governor of Nova Scotia.

I am glad to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) present tonight, because I am sure he will take a broad and proper view of this question. It gives me great pleasure to endorse the views of my hon. colleague from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. McLean). I listened attentively to the statement of the Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes) and I noticed that he said that ' anybody responding to a legal call ' would be recognized by him. Later, changing the phraseology a little, he said * anybody acting under a legal eaU. would be recognized under the Act as entitled to the 'bounty. There can be no question but that these men Of Prince Edward Island volunteered and drilled in preparation to repel an invasion, and that in doing so they were * responding to legal call.' That call was in the statute of the province. I may say to the Prime Minister, as he was not here the other evening when this matter was under discussion, that when the legislature of Prince Edward Island was called together in that year, the governor in his Speech from the Throne called the attention of the legislature to the fact that 'the British provinces were threatened with in-, vasion by men living in the republic to the south, and asked the legislature to make ail necessary provision to repel that invasion. In reply they said they would certainly make all necessary provision. I think it would be well to read one paragraph of the reply to the Speech from the Throne on that occasion:
It is with feelings of just pride that we have observed the loyalty and spirit evinced by our fellow-subjects in the neighbouring provinces when threatened by piratical attacks at the hands of lawless men; and we beg to assure your Excellency that should a similar emergency ever unfortunately occur in this Island, your Excellency could rely with confidence on a like spirit in its inhabitants of every creed and station; and we admit the necessity of doing all in our power towards making due preparation for such an emergency by earnestly considering the laws by which the militia and volunteer forces are at present regulated.
Then they proceeded to pass special legislation calling upon every man in the province from sixteen years to sixty to volunteer for service. In fact, they were obliged to enroll themselves, and nearly all male persons within the age limit did enroll themselves, at very great inconvenience, because there was no pay in the matter and they had to provide their own food. I might also refer to the statement

made by the hon. member for Queens that tlie legislature passed a resolution placing the whole revenue of the province at the disposal of the governor. That resolution was passed unanimously. It was moved) by the Solicitor General in these words:
Resolved, that, in consequence of the threatened invasion of the British colonies by bands of Fenian marauders, this House, pledges itself to place the whole of the revenue of the Island at the disposal of the Government for the purpose of organizing the militia and volunteers, and for such other military purposes as may be deemed expedient for the protection and defence of the colony.
There could not be anything more done by anybody-certainly nothing more was done in any province of the Dominion than was done by Prince Edward Island. The Minister of Militia, I think, stated, if nojt this evening, then a few evenings ago when this matter was under consideration, that we were somewhat late in preparing bo repel the threatened invasion. I find that the proclamation issued in the province of Nova Scotia was not withdrawn until thei 15th of May, 1866.
The people of Prince Edward Island prepared on April 14, under this resolution to defend the colony, so that they were well within the time they took action at least a month before the proclamation was withdrawn in Nova Scotia. I do not supposed that the Government would wish to take advantage of any technicality in regard to this matter; the Act is intended to apply to everybody who is entitled to take advantage of this legislation. I presume that is the case; if not, it is improper legislation. I hope that the Government will accept the suggestion made by the hon member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, and amend the Act so that it will apply to Prince Edward Island in the same way that it applies to the province of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The intention of the Bill is to apply this bounty to those who were actually called out for active service and who really turned out in response to that call. We all agree that the action of the legislature of Prince Edward Island was both patriotic and commendable, but as a matter of fact it does not seem to me that it brings the entire population of the Island within certain ages, as included in the terms of the resolution, within the scope of this Bill, for the reason that it was merely a resolution and that, although after legislation had been enacted, if it were enacted, the inhabitants of Prince Edward 2751
*Island may have drilled, it was not in respect of the occasion for which the militia of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the province of Canada put themselves in active service for the purpose of repelling invasion.
The Prime Minister is certainly mistaken in that; it was just for that very purpose that the special Act was passed and it was under that Act that the men drilled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When did they begin to drill?

I do not know the exact date.
Mr. A. A. McLEAlS : I think they were first called out on January 17, 1866, and they were out also after the Act was passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With the details of the whole situation I am not thoroughly familiar, but the resolution from which my hon. friend read a moment ago alluded to an emergency of some kind. It declared that if an emergency should arise in the future the resources of the province would be pledged for the purpose of dealing with it. It does not seem that that was dealing with an emergency which had been for some time in existence in the neighbouring province.
Eut they refer to that special emergency with which the province and the whole of Canada was then threatened.

The resolution says:
That in consequence of the threatened invasion of the British colonies by bands of Fenian marauders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That in consequence of the threatened invasion of the British colonies by bands of Fenian marauders, this House pledges itself to place the whole of the revenue of the Island at the disposal of the Government for the purpose of organizing the militia and volunteers, and for such other military purposes as may be deemed expedient for the protection and defence of the colony.
That was passed on April 14, 1866. The emergency which is alluded to, and which seems to have arisen in connection with the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, had arised some time before. In those provinces the procedure was not that of providing a militia which would in the future be prepared to deal with such an emergency, but that of the calling out of militia actually in existence under the

law of the province for the purpose of dealing with an emergency which was then imminent. My hon. friend suggests that this Act should be applied to the population of Prince Edward Island, which had then not been organized for militia purposes, and which, therefore, could not be called out for the purpose.
I am suggesting that it apply only to those who actually drilled and who actually responded to *the call; I did not mean the whole population of the province.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the other provinces of Canada there is no pretense of applying these bounties to those who had been drilling in January or in the previous year, or to those who drilled later in the year. The bounty is applied only to those who, being part of the active militia in those colonies, did actually, under the law of the land, by reason of the proclamation of the Governor, turn out on that particular occasion for the purpose of repelling invasion. My difficulty in regard to the matter so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, is that it does not appear that any condition of a like character existed in Prince Edward Island; that the men were not called out.
Were they not called out by Act of Parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They were called out in Nova Scotia by a proclamation -which it was possible for the Government to issue under the law of the land, and the bounty is being paid in the province of Nova Scotia only to those persons, who, being members of the active militia, turned out for active service in obedience to the proclamation of the Lieutenant Governor. There seems, therefore to be a very marked and clear distinction between the two cases. So far as 1870 is concerned, I do not think that any one in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Ontario could possibly receive any benefit in respect of the bounty as it applies to the year 1870. because although there was apprehended invasion, it was not an invasion which closely affected these particular provinces; it applied principally to the province of Quebec and to a small portion of the province of Ontario. There is no doubt that the men who drilled in those provinces during that year cannot receive any benefit from this bounty, although they would have been prepared to resist and doubtless would have been called out if invasion were imminent. It seems to me that the difficulty with regard to the case of Prince Edward Island

is that it does not fall within the very clear and definite principle to which I have alluded, that is, that the militia of Prince Edward Island, if any militia organization existed at that time, were not called out under the exigency of the law to resist and repel an apprehended invasion.

The Prime Minister says that they were not called out by the Governor's proclamation. This Bill does not require that they should be called out by the Governor's proclamation; it says by the Government.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: I think that the hon. gentleman possibly misunderstands the position. In Nova Scotia they had a Militia Act while in Prince Edward Island they had not.

Oh yes they had one passed in 1865.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: This resolution of 1865 merely proceeded to organize the militia forces. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick militia forces had been already organized and the proclamation in Nova Scotia was calling these men out for active service. There was no such proclamation in Prince Edward Island. Both of the members from the Island admit that; therefore whatever may be thought proper for some other occasions, I do not think they would come.
M. J. J. HUGHES: There was no actual service in Nova Scotia.
Mr SAM. HUGHES: Oh yes there was active service. They were called out to repel invasion. There is annual drill of the militia. But supposing there is an invasion or that men are called out for any other purpose than annual drill, that is active service. They are technical terms. That is why we include active service in the Bill, in order to eliminate the annual drill.

That is the very
thing that was done in Prince Edward Island. A special Act was passed, special provision was made for that occasion and it was not annual drill. If it was annual drill I could understand the position taken by the minister, but for this special purpose a special Act was passed and they were called out by the Governor. If that is not calling out, I do not know what would be.

My name has been mentioned in connection with this matter and I might make one statement. In the first place, I never made the statement that every man of the 15,000 odd applicants for

this bounty in Nova Scotia perjured himself, and I was rather surprised that certain members of the House used that word. I think the statement was made by one member during a former discussion that I had practically charged the men in Nova Scotia with having committed perjury. I think I know my duty as a member of Parliament and I know the condition of affairs in Nova Scotia well enough not to make such a broad statement as that. I did state that I believed very large numbers of people were receiving this bounty who were mere lads in 1866, and I do not wish to recede from that position a particle. I stated it was a scandal of the first magnitude.

Did the hon. member
say that nearly every able-bodied man in Nova Scotia claimed he was entitled to the bounty?

I have no recollection of making such a statement, although I have not my remarks before me. I do not think I made that statement because it would not have been true. There are thousands of able-bodied men in Nova Scotia to-day who were not born in 1866, and I certainly never made any such statement, at least I did not intend to. What I intended to say was that practically every able-bodied man of that time who was now living was claiming the bounty, and I think I am correct in that. I said it was a scandal, and I repeat it, that such an enormous proportion of the population of Nova Scotia should be paid $100 each for practically doing no more than turning out and performing their annual drill. While the Minister may draw a technical distinction between drilling in March and drilling in July, it is only a technicality. If the House or the minister want evidence of the truth of the suggestion I made it is contained in the letter read, by the member for Guysborough purporting to have been written by Mr. McLeod, the Conservative candidate in Victoria. I do not care whether Mr. McLeod wrote that letter or whether it was written for him; whoever WTote it had in the back of his head about the same idea that I have in my head, that there are many people in Nova Scotia to-day demanding, and I am afraid receiving, this bounty of $100 who did not feel that they were doing very much towards defending their country from the threatened invasion in 1866. To show that it is a scandal as administered you have only to take the rest of Canada. You do not hear of such
wholesale payments in the rest of Canada, and every discussion in this House during this session and last session tended to revert back to Nova Scotia. You did not hear about Ontario, Quebec or New Brunswick, it is all Nova Scotia and it is because the Act is being administered there in a way that is practically a scandal. While the minister may hide behind a technical definition of ' calling out,' he must feel in his mind that he is heartily ashamed of this legislation and of the way it is being administered in Nova Scotia. If he were to apply the law to Nova Scotia in the same spirit as he is applying it to the rest of Canada, no harm would be done. Personally, as I have said on many occasions, I do not believe in the principle; but once you adopt the principle I think the minister has very fairly indeed administered the law in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick. He has been narrow in many cases and cases have been pointed out wherein he should have been broader and should have included men who actually went to the front, no matter whether they belonged to a regular regiment of militia or not. Where he has erred in the other provinces in being too narrow in interpreting the law he has erred in Nova Scotia in throwing the doors wide open.

The hon. member says
that the administration of this law in Nova Scotia is a scandal. Would he be good enough to point out wherein it is a scandal and is being improperly administered?

It is a scandal in this, that because the Governor of the province of Nova Scotia was seized of the idea that it was his duty to issue a proclamation calling upon practically .every able-bodied man in the province from 16 to 60 years of age, at this last date, forty-eight years afterwards, men who never saw the possibility of danger, who never left their homes except to go to the ordinary headquarters of their regiments for their annual drill, are receiving $100 apiece from this country. I think I am justified in saying that it is a scandal. To show my hon. friend the proportions of this scandal, if the same routine proceeding had been followed in the rest of Canada at the time of the threatened invasion as was followed by the Governor of Nova Scotia there would have been paid out under this Act, not a million and a half of dollars, but six or seven million dollars. That is what it amounts to. Is not that a scandal?
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: No.

That is my answer to
my hon. friend from Cumberland. I do not go back on what I have said, and I have no desire to. I am prepared to accept responsibility for the statements I have made before the people of this country, and I am prepared to go to Nova Scotia and repeat the statements I have made to-hight and during the course of this debate. I had a letter a few days ago, not from the constituency of my hon. friend from Kings, N.S., but from Bridgetown, taking me to task for statements I was alleged to have made in connection with this matter. It was from one of the veterans, as they call themselves. I replied, and did not mince matters a particle. I told him exactly what I thought about it and exactly what I have said in Parliament, and gave him my views about good citizenship. I was delighted to receive a letter from him to-day in which he practically concurs in my views. That is a little evidence that the people of Nova; Scotia are amenable to reason. I would bet delighted to place my views before the people of Nova Scotia. If my hon. friend from Kings, N.S., would like to see the correspondence I will be glad to show it to him. I felt it my duty to make myself plain in regard to this matter, and I think it would be better if others did the same. I atm sorry the minister is extending the time to the last day of July next, rather than the last day of December. I would say, cut it down to the earliest possible moment. (Jet rid of the thing and let us forget it, ber cause it is not something on which the Minister of Militia will look back with any great amount of pride or glory when he comes to write his autobiography.
Mr. SAM. HUGM&ES:	I had agreed to
make it the end of December, but Mr1.' Panet came to me and said that by issuing the warrants as rapidly as possible the business could not be disposed of by the; end of the year. He asked for another year. We talked it over, and eventually compromised on the 31st of July. I do not want to go into any explanation as to why this iwas done, except to say that it 'was asked for by the veterans.
The same thing applies to Prince Edward Island.

I wish to say a few words in regard to a number of veterans in the county which I represent. As this is a matter that is going to be dealt with in history and literature, according to the minister, I wish to say a word or two in behalf of these men who have been refused the $100 grant that has been given in other cases. I also wish to correct the hon. member for Carieton when he says there are no complaints from Ontario, and that the complaints are confined almost entirely to Nova Scotia. I think we have already heard from hon. gentleman representing constituencies in Ontario. If I recollect aright, the hon. member for North Grey spoke on behalf of a number of people in his constituency, and so did the hon. member for North Perth and the hon. membeT for Glengarry. I have here letters from a number of old men in the riding which I represent. When the outbreak occurred and the regiments were called out, a number of these men went to join the Tillson-burg Company, but found it filled. They immediately endeavoured to join the company in the next town, Ingersoll, but that was also filled, so they immediately formed a company at Mount Elgin, which was known as Company No. 10 of the Oxford Rifles. They went to the county town and were supplied with rifles and uniforms and they remained on duty for a considerable period. It appears from ime records of the Militia Department that this company was not officially recognized

until the 17th of August, 1866. As a matter of fact, these men had been supplied with uniforms and rifles and were ready and anxious to serve their country. They 'found that the local regiments were filled, and they showed enough manliness and [DOT]spirit to organize a company of their own commanded by Captain Hagle and Lieut-' enant Chambers. The captain and lieutenant are both dead now, but about half a dozen of that same company are alive and in the riding at the present time. When the province of Ontario recognized the services that had been rendered to the country by the volunteers-ia number of years before it was recognized by the federal Government-these men received the provincial grant of 160 acres and also their medals as veterans of 1866, but when they made application for the $100 grants that the Government of Canada is giving they were turned down. They feeel it keenly, not so much for the sake of the $100, although I know some of them to whom it would be very welcome, but they feel that a reflection has been cast on them that they were not actual veterans of that occasion. On their behalf, I wish to enter my protest and say that if there is going to be any wider recognition of the people of Canada who responded to the call of their country in 1866, it should certainly cover the cases I have referred to.
, iMt. McKENZIE : I am sorry to take up the time of the House, but I shall direct my attention to the terms of the Bill itself. I may have to say something about the speech of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens. I am very sorry that a man of his years and discretion and cool [DOT]headedness should think it worth while on this occasion to throw down the gauntlet of political controversy. I am sorry it is only from the fair province of Nova Scotia that there seems to be any political wrangling about this matter. It is rather satisfactory, I presume, to the people of New Brunswick that there has been no wrangling at all over that province although it has its representatives on both sides of the House. The same thing is true of Ontario. The great province of Ontario, I understand, has participated largely in the benefits accruing from this Act. There are men sitting in this House on both sides of politics from the province of Ontario, but I am pleased to notice that no political controversies have been worked up in connection with this Bill. I do not know whether the people of Quebec participate in the
benefit of this Act or not, but if they do there is certainly no political controversy. I rather regret that it remains for us from the province of Nova Scotia to be wrangling politically over the virtues of this particular Act. I must say that, to the credit of the minister, he has possibly happened to live in the fulness of time. We must agree that there is development in all lines of thought in this country. Parliament has developed in thought; matters that would not receive the consideration of this House fifty years ago are now receiving consideration. Ideas have developed, and we are passing legislation to-day that possibly would not have received recognition in this country several years ago. Yet the fact that such legislation was not passed ten, fifteen or twenty years ago, that because in those days another Government was in power and they did not pass this Act, does not mean that they are to be condemned for it, because to so condemn them would not be consistent with the development of which I spoke. If parties are to be condemned for things they did not do, how does my hon. friend from Queens and Shelburne account for the twenty-two years during which the Conservative Government did nothing in connection with the subject that is engaging our attention? Sir John Macdonald and his party were in power during the first four years after 1866, when the heroism of these volunteers would be fresh in the minds of the people. Sir John Macdonald and his associates did not think it necessary to do anything in connection with this matter. In 1878 that famous statesman again came to the head of affairs in Canada and continued in that position until the time of his death sixteen or seventeen years afterwards, and during the whole of his career it did not occur to him that it was necessary to do anything in connection with this matter. If there be any virtue in connection with this question, and I suppose there must be some virtue in connection with it or it would not receive the attention of the present Minister of Militia, surely such a statesman, such a true representative of the public thought of the country, as Sir John Macdonald, would have thought about it and would have given some material effect to his ideas in regard to it. He did not do so; but are the people of Canada to put a black mark against the history of that great statesman and to say that he was no good and had no kindly thought for the veterans of Canada because he did not do anything far them? If that could not be said about Sir John Macdonald, it should

not be said about any other statesman who occupied a similar position in later years. It so happens that this idea developed in the days of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), and his Minister of Militia, and this little act of kindness has been done by them to these veterans. I do not suppose that it would occur to the Minister of Militia that he was going to raise any political contention when he introduced this Bill; at all events, I hope it was not his idea. I had a better opinion of the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne than to suppose that he would again try to make political capital out of this matter when we were hoping to get away and hoping that all contentious questions would be dropped. As for myself, if it is the intention of the hon. member to come down to Victoria and try to defeat me by the speech which he has made to-night, he is	perfectly welcome to any capital
he can make out of it.	When
the question took concrete shape in this House, I supported the legislation. I spoke for it and voted for it. I assisted my people, who were entitled, to get this bounty and I think the whole of them got it who were entitled to it. I must say in respect to my horn, friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) that he is entitled to his own views .about this matter as to whether or not there is a scandal in Nova Scotia in connection. with it. I believe that every man in Nova Scotia who is receiving a dollar of this money is receiving it actuality and altogether within the law and because he is entitled to it. (Last summer I made out quite a number of applications myself. In one district in my county, the grand, old, Scotch district of Grand Narrows, I attended for the convenience of the old veterans so as to take their applications. I met about fifty of these men averaging from 75 to 115 years of age. I met one veteran by the name of Stephen McDougall who was 115 years of age. He was able to walk out a mile or two to the little store where I had my meeting with these people.
One hundred and fifteen was it?
One hundred and fifteen years of age, and I am glad to know-
I saw several of the old section books, with the names of the men that my hon. friend refers to all written in it and the different drills that they attended.

It was a pleasure to
me to know that this old gentleman received $100. I regret to say that I understand he died since but still this $100 would help to give him a decent burial and to make some other preparations that he would perhaps not have been able to make had he not received this $100. I do not think there is very much fault to be found with this Act in Nova Scotia. This is only a sample of what was happening in other parts of the province and it is a sample of the way in which this Act brought some sunshine and gladness into the lives of these old men by giving them this money to which they were entitled at a time perhaps when they were not able to earn much money in any other way. It was all done in four or five hours and I received the applications of some forty-five or fifty people. I know nothing which gave me greater pleasure than to be able to serve the old men and I felt when I had the opportunity I would give to the minister an expression of the pleasure that I had in being -his officer in carrying out the provisions of the Act in that particular respect. While I am never averse to a scrap even with the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne or of any other hon. member when the occasion requires, I must say that I am not in any scrapping mood to-night.
The particular purpose I had in getting up was to urge upon the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia the fairness and equity of extending this Act so .as to cover the cases of veterans' widows who may now be living.
It may strike the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia that we have had enough of this, and that we should not be bothered any longer, and that, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Oarleton (Mr. Carvell) is scenting other scandals, we should not give him any opportunity, so far as Nova Scotia is concerned. A right to this recognition by Canada was earned the moment the act was performed in 1866, and it has existed ever since, and it was recognized in 1912. The mere fact that one veteran died and another lived does not make the slightest difference; the service to his country existed ever since the date of the Fenian raid. If a man is dead and has left, perhaps, an aged and decrepid widow, why should not this recognition enure to her benefit. I have had old women coming to my office last summer and the summer before, some of them blind

and led by the hand by their grandchildren, asking about the Minister of Militia, and I was pleased to tell them that he *was always in the pink of condition, and then they asked if this Act applied to them, *and they told me that their husbands had *died, some of them years ago, and some only in the middle of March, 1912, and it .pained me to have to tell them that they did not come under the operation of the Act. 1 submit to the Minister of Militia [DOT]that if this recognition was due to a man who was alive on the 1st of April, 1912, in virtue of his services Tendered in 1866, the right of the family of the veteran who died before the 1st of April, 1912, is equally [DOT]strong. Any lawyer in this House will [DOT]agree with me that, on the facts, a jury [DOT]would find that the family of the man who died before the 1st of April, 1912, was [DOT]equally entitled to this recognition as the [DOT]family of the man who had had the good [DOT]luck to live longer.
It is extremely disagreeable that political cantankerousness has been introduced into this matter, and particularly by a mild-mannered man like the hon.
12 m. member for Queens-Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy). It only shows ho.w deep-rooted this thing is among the rank and file of our Conservative friends in Nova Scotia, when they had to bring out in such an unusual role the gentleman whom they put forward to-night as their champion. I would not have paid so much attention to it if it had broken out from several gentlemen who are never averse to throwing stones across the floor; but coming from the quarter it did it showed how deep-TOoted the feeling is. I point out to the minister that there never has been an election in Nova Scotia since this Act was passed, in which it did not do service. We have repeatedly seen letters with great big red seals on them, purporting to come from Ottawa, and we have heard the holder of these red seals saying to the people: I have received this from the Minister of Militia, you know I am recognized in this district as the official representative of the Borden Administration; the minister has sent me this list for my approval, you made application and he does not know whether you are entitled to the money or not, and so he sent me this for verification, if I approve of your name you get the money and if I do not you will not get it, if you vote for my man in the elections I will give my approval and you will get the money, but if you do not I will put a cross opposite your name and that will show you are not entitled to
it. That is the way this thing has been done. Therefore, I am sure the Minister of Militia and the Prime Minister will excuse us if we are getting tired of this sort of thing. We had it carried even a little further in the election in Victoria last year, when this McLeod letter was paraded all over the county. [DOT]The first part of the letter is that this gentleman, Mr. McLeod, is in possession of information from Ottawa as to who will and who will not get Fenian Raid money. [DOT]And he says there is a report-a report from where? We have the right to believe that it was a report from Ottawa-that you made a false statement in making your .application and there may be some trouble '-quite possibly there may be a prosecution for perjury; but I can assure you that if you are my friend nothing shall come of [DOT]it. I submit that this is a most extraordinary statement for a candidate for the suffrages of the electors to make on the eve of an election. It is bribery; it is a corrupt act. But it is likely to be dealt with in another way. I call the attention of the Minister of Militia to the way his good intentions towards the veterans of [DOT]Nova Scotia are being used in this connection. My good friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) came to the fore with the statement that Mr. McLeod did not intend [DOT]what would ordinarily be read from this [DOT]language. The hon. gentleman was not in the county of Victoria at the time of the election, or he would have known very differently. He would have known that this letter was sent broadcast throughout the county by the agents, on foot and on horseback, of Mr. McLeod-agents who went from house to house, and who fo1-lowed the people telling them that they had information that these people had committed perjury, and if the people did not vote as the agents wanted them to [DOT]vote, prosecutions would follow, but if they voted right no prosecutions would follow. And on nomination day, in the town of [DOT]Baddeck, that was put up to one of the men who had made that statement-it was put up to him that he had been canvassing in this style. He was pressed with it on nomination day and did not deny it. If my statement is questioned by any hon. gentleman opposite, that hon. gentleman can learn who the man was to whom this question was put up if he will inquire of Mr. Rowlings or Dr. Hayes. These are the things that we had to contend against. Now, I want to press this a little closer,

perhaps, to the Prime Minister, and tell him why Mr. MeLeod and some of the other gentlemen associated with him in the drafting of this letter ventured to state that men could commit perjury and escape. They could well point out that there was a man in the county of Richmond, an officer of the right hon. gentleman's Government, who committed forgery and was sent to jail, or penitentiary I have forgotten which, and he was in only half his time when he was released. They could say: We have a most excellent and convenient Department of Justice, with a most pious and excellent man at the head of it; and if you tell him the proper story, he will let your man out-no matter about the perjury business, we have an institution above the courts and all the little powers in Nova Scotia that protects our friends. And they could say also:	There
was a man in Sydney about two years ago who was found guilty of perjury and sent to penitentiary for three years, but when he had served less than half that time, we got him out; we appealed to the DepaTt-1 ment of Justice at Ottawa and told our little story; we used our .political pull-and out he came. So that Mr. McLeod and his friends in this contest in Victoria county, when they were throwing broadcast this literature saying that people would be immune from prosecution for perjury if the voted the right way, were talking by the book, talking with authority, talking of something they knew about.
